AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: What the Word AI Actually Covers
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Programs whose rules a person wrote, and programs that pulled the rules out of data. Separating the layers packed into a single word.
objectives: Tell apart how rule-based programs and machine learning work
Map how artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI contain one another
Distinguish two systems that look identical from the outside by their structure

steps.title: Same Window, Different Machine
steps.contentMarkdown:
Open the help window on a retail site and buttons usually come first. Track an order. Start a return. Ask about billing. Press one and a message someone wrote in advance appears word for word. Type a question that no button covers and the window loops back to asking how it can help.

A recent chatbot accepts any sentence at all. Faced with a question it has never seen, it composes a new answer. The answer is not always correct, but it is always a well-formed answer.

The two windows look the same. What happens inside them is the opposite. The first walks a path someone laid down in advance. The second builds a path on the spot.

Hold on to that difference before going further. The word AI covers so much ground that trading the label back and forth, without knowing what sits behind it, produces conversations that never touch anything.

steps.title: Who Writes the Rules
steps.contentMarkdown:
Spam filtering shows the two approaches side by side.

**Rule-based** filtering means a person writes out every condition. Block the message if the subject line contains free. Block it if the sender appears on this list. The conditions are explicit and it is easy to say why a message was caught. The cost shows up when a spammer types f r e e with spaces and the message sails through. Someone has to sit down and add one more condition.

**Machine learning** does not have a person write the conditions. You hand over hundreds of thousands of messages labeled spam and hundreds of thousands labeled legitimate, then let the program work out the rule that separates them. What comes out is not one word like free but a pattern that mixes word combinations, the number of links, and even the hour the message was sent.

Does a person write the rules, or do the rules come out of the data. That fork is the definition of machine learning.
steps.imageAlt: A workbench where the same pebbles are sorted by a fixed hole rule on the left and by comparison with three shape examples on the right

steps.title: Four Nested Circles
steps.contentMarkdown:
Many people line up AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI as four items of equal standing. They are not side by side. They sit inside one another.

| Layer | What it covers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Artificial intelligence | Any technique that stands in for human judgment | Rule-based diagnostic programs |
| Machine learning | The part of it that finds rules in data | Spam classification, demand forecasting |
| Deep learning | The part of that built from neural networks stacked deep | Face recognition, translation |
| Generative AI | The part of that which produces new output | Chatbots, image generation |

The diagnostic programs hospitals used in the 1980s were called artificial intelligence too. They were thousands of conditional statements written by hand, and they learned nothing. The AI in today's news usually means the innermost circle, the generative one.

Reach for an example from the outer circle to explain the inner one, or the reverse, and the explanation stops matching the thing being explained.

steps.title: Recognizing Versus Producing
steps.contentMarkdown:
The first thing deep learning got good at was **recognizing**. Look at a photo and decide whether it shows a cat or a dog. Read handwriting and turn it into digits. Turn speech into text. The answer comes from a fixed set of options, so scoring is straightforward. The shift began in earnest when a neural network cut the error rate sharply at the 2012 image recognition competition.

**Producing** is hard to score in the first place. Ask for a new drawing of a cat and there is no correct answer. Endlessly many plausible drawings exist, and which one is better varies from person to person.

Generation became possible anyway because the problem was rewritten as predicting what comes next. Predict the next word. Predict the next pixel. Predict what the image looks like with the noise stripped away. String enough predictions together and a finished result appears.

Keeping recognition and production apart makes the lessons that follow much easier.

steps.title: What to Ask When Something Is Labeled AI
steps.contentMarkdown:
A product page that says AI tells you nothing about what is inside. The label gets attached to a hundred lines of conditional logic often enough. Since the name settles nothing, it helps to keep a short list of checks.

- Is the output identical every time, or does it vary. Identical output for identical input points toward a rule-based system.
- Does it handle input it has never seen. Watch what happens when you step outside the prepared list.
- Does anyone say what it learned from. The character of the training material sets the character of the output.
- What happens when it is wrong. Look for a step where a person checks the result.

This course deals with the innermost circle, generative AI. Starting with the next lesson, it opens up training and inference, neural networks, tokens, and attention in turn. Once you know how they work, you can decide for yourself how far to trust the output.

quiz.question: Where does machine learning part ways with a rule-based program?
choices: It processes input faster
Instead of a person writing the rules, the rules are found in data
It requires an internet connection
Its results are easier to explain
quiz.explanation: In a rule-based system a person writes the conditions by hand. Machine learning receives example data and lets the program work out the rule that separates the categories.

quiz.question: Which statement describes the relationship among artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI?
choices: They are four separate technologies with no overlap
Generative AI is the broadest and artificial intelligence the narrowest
Machine learning sits inside artificial intelligence, deep learning inside machine learning, and generative AI inside deep learning
Deep learning and machine learning mean the same thing
quiz.explanation: The four layers are nested rather than parallel. Artificial intelligence is the outermost circle and generative AI the innermost.

quiz.question: How does generative AI produce output when no single correct answer exists?
choices: It picks the closest match from results prepared in advance
It rewrites the task as predicting what comes next and chains those predictions together
It runs through rules a person laid out, in order
It copies results found on the internet without changing them
quiz.explanation: Generation is hard to score directly. The task gets rewritten as predicting the next word or the next pixel, and those predictions are chained into a finished result.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Training and Inference Are Different Jobs
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: The time spent building a model and the time spent using it are fully separate. Why a conversation never turns into skill.
objectives: Understand where and how training and inference divide
Explain the difference between generalization and overfitting with an example
Judge the limits created by a knowledge cutoff

steps.title: Two Clocks
steps.contentMarkdown:
Generative AI runs on two stages that operate at completely different timescales.

**Training** is the stage that builds the model. Large numbers of machines run together for weeks or months. When the stage ends, the numbers inside the model are frozen in place.

**Inference** is the stage where a user sends a question and receives an answer. It finishes in seconds. Not a single number inside the model changes during it. The frozen numbers simply pass the input through and an answer comes out.

One way to picture it: training is compiling a dictionary, inference is opening one to look something up. Open the dictionary a hundred times and its contents stay exactly as they were.

Blur these two stages together and every effect described below gets misread.
steps.imageAlt: One metalworking factory with slow steel die making in the rear and repeated stamping from the finished die in front

steps.title: A Conversation Does Not Become Skill
steps.contentMarkdown:
Point out a wrong answer to a chatbot and correct it, and the correction holds for that conversation. Open a new conversation, ask the same question, and the wrong answer is back.

The correction was not ignored. It was alive only inside the context of that conversation. Nothing about the model changes during inference, so once the window closes, the correction leaves nothing behind in the model.

Memory features in consumer services are not a way of editing the model either. They store what you said somewhere separate and paste it back in at the front of the next conversation. From the model's side, it is context being read fresh each time.

Conversations with users do sometimes feed into a later round of training. But that is a story about a new model built months from now, not about anything happening in the conversation in front of you.

steps.title: Memorized Versus Learned
steps.contentMarkdown:
The goal of training is not to score well on the training material. It is to handle input the model has never seen, which is called **generalization**.

Picture a student who memorized a hundred past exam papers along with their answer keys. Hand back a past paper and the score is perfect. Hand over a fresh question and everything falls apart, because what got memorized was where the answers sat, not how to solve anything. That state is called **overfitting**.

This is why training material gets split. Most of it goes into learning, and a portion is held back and brought out as a test. When the score on the learning material keeps climbing while the score on the held-back portion starts to fall, that is the signal that memorization is taking over.

There is a failure in the other direction as well. A model too simple for the task never picks up the rule at all. It has neither memorized nor learned.

steps.title: Knowledge Has a Cutoff Date
steps.contentMarkdown:
Collecting training material stops at some point in time. Anything that happened after it is not inside the model. That point is the **knowledge cutoff**.

Ask about an event past the cutoff and one of two things comes back. The model says it does not know, or it makes something up as though it knew. The second is the dangerous one. Information near the cutoff is especially faint, while the tone of voice stays just as confident.

Services with search attached step past this limit. Given a question, they look up web pages or internal documents, read them, and answer from what they read. The answer rests on material just retrieved rather than on memory inside the model.

So when the question involves recent facts, it is worth checking whether search is attached. If it is not, do not hand over questions that hinge on dates.

steps.title: The Material Shapes the Output
steps.contentMarkdown:
What went into the training material largely determines what the output is like.

English material dominates by a wide margin, so the same question asked in English and asked in another language can come back with noticeably different depth. Subjects that live mostly in one language's sources, such as a country's modern history or its domestic regulations, blur easily.

The same split runs across fields. Topics with a large pile of writing on the open internet get answered down to the details. Topics that exist mainly in academic papers or paywalled archives get skimmed.

There is a way to check. Look at whether the answer is specific. See whether names, years, and event titles appear, then verify those directly. When nothing but vague description keeps coming, read it as a sign that the material on that topic was thin.

quiz.question: Why does the same mistake come back in a new conversation?
choices: The feature that saves corrections is switched off
Nothing inside the model changes during inference
The model judged the correction to be wrong
Conversation logs are encrypted and cannot be read
quiz.explanation: The moment a user is typing is inference. The values inside the model are fixed then, so a correction stays alive only inside the context of that conversation.

quiz.question: Which situation describes overfitting?
choices: Scores are high on the material used for learning but drop on material the model has not seen
Scores are evenly high on both the learning material and new material
Training runs far too slowly
The model is too large to store
quiz.explanation: Overfitting means the material got memorized instead of the method learned. You spot it when the score on learning material and the score on new material come apart.

quiz.question: What is the safest choice when asking about facts from after the knowledge cutoff?
choices: Ask the same question several times in a row
Request a longer answer
Work in a setup with search or document lookup and take the sources along with the answer
Switch the question to English
quiz.explanation: Events past the cutoff are not inside the model. It is safer to work where the system reads retrieved material to answer, and to receive the sources so you can check them.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: A Neural Network Is a Bundle of Arithmetic
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Units that multiply, add, and filter, stacked into layers. Learning means nudging the numbers inside them.
objectives: Describe in plain words what a single artificial neuron computes
Grasp what changes when layers are stacked deep
Understand learning as a process of adjusting weights

steps.title: A Name Borrowed From the Brain
steps.contentMarkdown:
The name neural network comes from the nerve cells of the brain. The borrowing stops at the name. How the brain actually works is still not fully understood, and a neural network is not an attempt to reproduce it.

What happens inside is multiplication and addition. It takes in numbers, multiplies each one by a different amount, adds the results, then passes the total through a filter on its way out. That single unit is called an artificial neuron.

The idea was already on the table in the 1950s, then sat buried for decades. The machines were too weak and there was too little material to learn from. Both conditions arrived in the 2010s and the idea came back up.

Strip away the phrase about thinking like a brain and what remains is a great deal of arithmetic. How that arithmetic is arranged is the whole story.

steps.title: What One Neuron Does
steps.contentMarkdown:
Think about reviewing a loan application. The reviewer looks at income, length of employment, and existing debt. Each item carries a different amount of weight. Income counts for a lot, length of employment for less. Score each item, multiply by its weight, add everything up, and approve the loan if the total clears a threshold.

That is what an artificial neuron does. It multiplies each input by a **weight**, adds the products, then adds one more value that acts as the threshold. The result goes through an **activation function**.

The activation function is the filter on the output. The common form is simple: push anything negative down to zero and let anything positive pass unchanged. Without this filter, stacking layer after layer collapses into a single multiplication. The filter is what lets the network handle problems that no straight line can separate.

steps.title: Why Layers Get Stacked
steps.contentMarkdown:
One neuron can only make a simple call. So you place many of them in a row and feed their results into the next row as input. That row is a **layer**. A network with many layers stacked up is called deep, and that is where the word deep learning comes from.

In face recognition, each layer picks up something different.

- First layer: boundaries between light and dark, short lines
- Middle layers: corners, curves, and textures formed where lines meet
- Later layers: parts such as eyes, nose, and mouth
- Final layer: the identity inferred from how those parts are arranged

Nobody tells the network to go find the eyes. Stack the layers, train it to get the answer right, and the middle layers take on those roles by themselves. This staircase, running from simple fragments up to complex concepts, is where the power of a deep network lives.
steps.imageAlt: A simple edge shadow passing through four physical mesh layers and assembling into a face on the final wall

steps.title: Learning Means Correcting Numbers
steps.contentMarkdown:
The weights in a freshly built network are meaningless values. Feed in a photo and something absurd comes out.

Learning runs in a loop.

1. Feed in an input and read off the answer.
2. Measure the error, meaning how far the answer sits from the correct one.
3. Nudge the weights by a very small amount in the direction that reduces the error.
4. Move to the next piece of material and repeat.

Step 3 works backward from the final layer, tracing how much each weight contributed to the error. That calculation is called **backpropagation**.

The trick is moving a little at a time instead of correcting hard in one go. Move too far and you overshoot the point of lowest error, and the values swing around. That step size is called the learning rate, one of a handful of settings a person chooses.

In the end, learning is repetitive work: pushing an enormous pile of numbers into place, a little at a time.

steps.title: Why the Inside Is Hard to Read
steps.contentMarkdown:
What a trained neural network leaves behind is its weights. In a large model the count runs past billions.

Each one is just a number. Saying in human terms why that number settled on that value is difficult. There is no structure you can point at the way you can say income carries the most weight in a loan review. The judgment is spread across billions of values.

That is how neural networks became systems that produce good results while offering no reason for them. In medicine, hiring, and lending, where a reason has to be given, this property becomes an obstacle.

Research into looking inside continues. Identifying which neurons respond to which concepts is one well-known line of work. It is still at the stage of explaining pieces, though, and nowhere near letting a person read the full path of a model's judgment.

quiz.question: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
choices: It compares the inputs against each other and keeps only the largest
It multiplies each input by a weight, adds the results, and passes them through an activation function
It looks each input up in a dictionary and substitutes the meaning
It shuffles the inputs at random and hands them to the next layer
quiz.explanation: It multiplies by weights, sums the products, adds a threshold value, then filters the result through an activation function on the way to the next layer. Without that filter, stacked layers collapse into a single multiplication.

quiz.question: In a face recognition network, how do the early layers differ from the later ones in what they pick up?
choices: The early layers see only color and the later ones only size
The early layers handle simple fragments such as lines and edges, the later ones complex concepts such as parts and identity
The early and later layers repeat exactly the same work
The early layers are specified by a person and the later ones settled by learning
quiz.explanation: As layers go deeper they climb from simple fragments toward complex concepts. Which layer takes which role is not specified by a person but settled during training.

quiz.question: Why are weights not moved by a large amount in a single step?
choices: Because it costs more to compute
Because storage would run short
Because it overshoots the point of lowest error and the values swing around
Because weights must never turn negative
quiz.explanation: A large step jumps past the point where the error is smallest, so the values never settle. The learning rate is kept small and the weights are pushed into place gradually.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: The Gate Where Text Becomes Numbers
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: A model does not handle characters. Both the bill and a whole family of mistakes are decided at the step that splits text into tokens and turns them into coordinates.
objectives: Understand what a token is and why the count differs across languages
Grasp how embeddings turn meaning into coordinates
Anticipate the mistakes that come from working in token units

steps.title: The Model Does Not See Letters
steps.contentMarkdown:
A neural network multiplies and adds. It accepts nothing but numbers. What a user types is text. A conversion step has to sit in between.

The simplest approach numbers every character. The letter a is 1, b is 2, and so on. This makes sentences extremely long, and each unit carries very little information.

Numbering every word runs into the opposite problem. The list grows without end and cannot cope with new coinages, typos, or proper nouns. A word missing from the list stops the process cold.

So the middle ground won out. Fragments that frequently appear together get bundled into one unit. That unit is called a **token**. It is smaller than a word and larger than a character.

steps.title: Tokens as Fragments
steps.contentMarkdown:
How text gets split into tokens is decided by which fragments showed up often in the training material. English dominated that material, so the split is efficient for English. A common English word bundles into a single token.

Korean works out differently. Writing the same meaning often costs several times as many tokens. Particles and endings attach to stems so the surface form keeps changing, and on top of that the splitting rules themselves were fitted to English.

That lands as real cost.

- Billing is usually counted in tokens. The same content can cost more in Korean than in English.
- How much text fits in one pass is also counted in tokens. A Korean document fits less inside the same limit.
- Output length caps run on tokens too, so a Korean answer can get cut off first.

Running the same job in English is sometimes cheaper and faster. The tone of the result still has to be reworked by a person afterward.

steps.title: Coordinates for Meaning
steps.contentMarkdown:
The number attached to a token is only an index. It carries no meaning. Nothing guarantees that token 3 and token 4 mean anything similar.

So the index gets converted again, into coordinates. A single token is represented as a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers. That list is called an **embedding**.

The coordinates come with one property. Tokens close in meaning sit close together. King and queen are near each other, Seoul and Tokyo are near each other, run and sprint are near each other. Nobody arranged this by hand. The positions settle that way during training.

That property changed search. Older search required the words to match character for character. With coordinates, cheap laptop and affordable notebook land near each other and both get caught by the same query. Search by meaning grew out of this.
steps.imageAlt: Related porcelain miniatures clustered on emerald felt with an unrelated boat isolated far away

steps.title: Arithmetic on the Coordinates
steps.contentMarkdown:
Once meaning lives in coordinates, it can be handled with arithmetic.

One example became famous in early embedding research. Take king, subtract man, add woman, and you land near queen. Take Paris, subtract France, add Japan, and Tokyo comes out nearby. The directions between coordinates carry relationships such as gender or capital city.

The example does not always come out that cleanly. A handful of cases that worked well got quoted widely, while plenty of relationships come out tangled. Treating the coordinate space as a dictionary that captures meaning perfectly overstates it.

In today's models the coordinates are not even fixed. Inside a sentence, the surrounding words change how the same token is represented. Whether bank means the edge of a river or a place that holds money is settled by context. The structure that handles that adjustment is attention, the subject of the next lesson.

steps.title: Mistakes That Tokens Create
steps.contentMarkdown:
Because the model sees the world in token units, it makes mistakes that look strange to a person.

**Counting letters.** Questions about how many times a given letter appears in a particular word go wrong often. The word is already bundled into a chunk, so the letters inside it are not visible one by one.

**Reversing and word games.** Arranging letters backward or peeling off the last letter is weak for the same reason.

**Numbers.** A long number gets split across several tokens and the place values scatter. Arithmetic is safer handed to a calculator or to executed code.

**Unusual spellings.** Notation mixed with special characters, heavy typos, and rare foreign words split into unfamiliar fragments and the handling wobbles.

When a job like this has to be done, change the shape of the request. Write the letters out separated by spaces, or have the counting itself run as code. Knowing the weak spot and routing around it beats repeating the same instruction.

quiz.question: Why does the same content take more tokens in Korean than in English?
choices: Because Korean carries more information per sentence than English
Because the token splitting rules were derived from English material
Because Korean characters were added to Unicode later
Because Korean requires the embedding to be computed twice
quiz.explanation: Token units are set from the fragments that appeared often in training material. English material dominated, so the split is efficient for English, while Korean with its attached particles and endings breaks into finer pieces.

quiz.question: What is the key property of an embedding?
choices: It sorts tokens into alphabetical order
Tokens close in meaning end up close together in the coordinate space
It compresses tokens to save storage
It attaches one correct answer to each token
quiz.explanation: An embedding turns a token into a list of numbers, that is, into coordinates. During training, tokens close in meaning settle near one another, and that property is what made search by meaning possible.

quiz.question: Why do questions about how many times a letter appears in a word go wrong so often?
choices: Because the model cannot perform arithmetic at all
Because the question is too short
Because the word is already bundled into a token, so the letters inside are not visible one by one
Because counting letters is a forbidden operation
quiz.explanation: The model sees input as tokens rather than characters. When a whole word forms one chunk, counting the individual letters inside it is difficult.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Attention: The Structure That Decides What to Look At
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Weights decide which word in a sentence should look at which other word. A look inside the structure that reset the field after 2017.
objectives: Explain with an example how attention handles context
Identify how the transformer differs from reading in sequence
Understand how parallel processing opened the way to scaling models

steps.title: How Do You Know Who He Is
steps.contentMarkdown:
Take one pair of sentences.

Daniel handed the book to his brother. He studied the cover for a long time.

The he in the second sentence is the brother. A person knows this without effort, because the situation reads as the person receiving the book looking at its cover rather than the person handing it over.

For a machine this is not easy. The token he carries no information on its own. Something has to decide which word in the previous sentence it connects to, and that decision changes from sentence to sentence.

**Attention** is what does this work. It computes how much the token being processed should draw on each of the other tokens in the sentence. Processing he assigns a high weight to brother and a low weight to book. The weights are not looked up in a fixed table. They are computed fresh for each sentence.
steps.imageAlt: A triangular scene just after Minsu hands his brother a blank book, with only the brother studying the cover

steps.title: How the Weights Get Computed
steps.contentMarkdown:
Attention builds three values with different roles for every token. A query from the side doing the looking, a key from the side being looked at, and the content actually handed over.

The query of the token being processed is matched against the keys of every other token. Whatever matches well receives a high weight. Content is then mixed and pulled in according to those weights. It resembles typing a search term at a library and getting material back ordered by relevance.

The calculation does not run only once. It splits into several branches computed at the same time. One branch tracks grammatical relations, another tracks what a pronoun refers to, another tracks the topic word. Layering several lines of sight like this is called multi-head attention.

Which branch watches what is not assigned by a person. The branches diverge during training.

steps.title: The Turn in 2017
steps.contentMarkdown:
Before that, the dominant approach read a sentence one word at a time, front to back. As it read, it updated a running summary and combined that summary with the next word. This family of models is called recurrent neural networks, or RNNs.

They had two weaknesses. Information from the beginning faded as sentences got longer. And the next word could not be processed until the previous one was finished, so the computation could not be divided up.

The transformer architecture published in 2017 dropped the recurrence and kept only attention. It lays the whole sentence out at once and lets the tokens reference each other. The first word and the last word connect directly, so distance stops being the problem.

Order information gets supplied separately. Attention alone cannot tell what came first, so a value marking each position is added to the embedding.

steps.title: The Scale That Parallelism Opened
steps.contentMarkdown:
The real impact of the transformer was not its accuracy but the fact that **the work can be divided up**.

With a structure that reads in sequence, attaching a hundred machines buys nothing. Nothing downstream starts until the step before it finishes, so the machines queue. A transformer handles the whole sentence at once, so adding machines makes it faster.

That opened the path to growing training material and model size together. Increase the material tenfold and the model tenfold and performance was observed to follow, and the competition ran in that direction.

There is a cost. Attention matches every token against every other token, so the expense climbs steeply as sentences get longer. That is why handling long documents is expensive. Work on reducing that cost continues.

steps.title: What Knowing Attention Buys You
steps.contentMarkdown:
Once you know the structure, several things you run into while using these systems have an explanation.

**Put important conditions at the start or the end.** Conditions buried in the middle of a long request have been reported to fade. Place the constraints that must hold at the beginning or the end.

**Feeding in a long document raises cost and time sharply.** The amount of computation grows close to the square of the token count. Excerpting only the part that matters pays off.

**Cutting vague references stabilizes the result.** Phrases such as it and the thing mentioned above leave room for attention to land on the wrong target. Writing the target out again is safer.

The next lesson looks at the moment after context has been worked out, the step where the answer actually gets built one token at a time.

quiz.question: What does attention do?
choices: It deletes unnecessary words from the sentence
It computes how much the token being processed should draw on each of the other tokens
It sorts the words into alphabetical order
It fixes the length of the sentence in advance
quiz.explanation: Attention computes how much the tokens should draw on one another. Those weights do not come from a fixed table but are computed fresh for every sentence.

quiz.question: Where does the transformer part ways with the earlier recurrent approach?
choices: It reads the words one at a time in order, front to back
It lays the whole sentence out at once and lets the tokens reference each other
It runs on rules alone with no training
It has no limit on sentence length whatsoever
quiz.explanation: The recurrent approach read front to back while updating a running summary. The transformer drops the recurrence, handles the whole sentence at once, and has the tokens reference each other directly.

quiz.question: Why do cost and time rise sharply when a long document is fed in?
choices: Because the document gets read through several times over
Because every token is matched against every other token, so computation swells steeply as length grows
Because long documents use separate storage
Because an extra translation step gets added
quiz.explanation: Attention matches every token against every other token, so the amount of computation grows close to the square of the length. Excerpting only the part that matters pays off.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: An Answer Assembled One Token at a Time
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: An answer does not arrive whole. It is what you get from picking one candidate out of a probability distribution and appending it, over and over, to the end.
objectives: Understand generation as repeated next-token prediction
Grasp how the randomness setting shapes the output
Know why the same question yields different answers, and what to do about it

steps.title: It Does Not Start Out Knowing the Answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
People usually start writing with some sense of where the conclusion is headed. A generative model does not.

The model performs exactly one calculation at a time: assigning probabilities to the tokens that could come after the text so far. It picks one from that distribution and appends it. The text is now one token longer. The longer text goes back in and the same calculation runs again. This repeats until a signal for the end appears.

While writing the first sentence it has no idea what the last sentence will be. What has already been written constrains what comes next strongly enough that the result holds together.

The screen where an answer trickles out character by character is not a visual effect. That is genuinely how it is being built.
steps.imageAlt: A mosaic artisan placing one tile at the end of a finished path with an unplanned blank floor and candidate pieces ahead

steps.title: Looking Inside the Distribution
steps.contentMarkdown:
What comes after the weather today is. The model scores every candidate.

| Candidate | Probability |
|---|---|
| fine | High |
| cloudy | Medium |
| cold | Medium |
| rectangular | Near zero |

Probabilities get assigned across the entire vocabulary. Most sit near zero while a small number of candidates split the large values.

How the pick happens here changes the result substantially. Always taking the top candidate keeps sentences safe but predictable. The same phrasing repeats, and the text sometimes circles the same clause.

Picking at random in proportion to probability produces more variety. It also brings the risk of an off candidate getting drawn. The dial that tunes this balance comes in the next step.

steps.title: The Randomness Dial
steps.contentMarkdown:
The most widely used setting is **temperature**. It controls how flat the probability distribution gets spread out.

- Lower the temperature and the distribution sharpens. Weight concentrates on high-probability candidates and the output stabilizes. This suits translation, summarizing, extracting data, and code, where accuracy matters.
- Raise the temperature and the distribution flattens. Lower-probability candidates get room to be drawn and the phrasing varies more. This suits brainstorming and producing several drafts. Push it too high and sentences come apart.

A few other settings play similar roles. Keeping only the top few candidates, and keeping candidates only until their cumulative probability reaches a set share, are the common ones.

In consumer interfaces the dial is hidden and the service picks a reasonable value. On a developer connection you set it yourself.

steps.title: Same Question, Different Answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
This is why the same question asked twice comes back differently. A step that picks at random among candidates sits in the middle of the process, so the paths diverge. Once one token differs, everything after it differs.

There are situations where this property becomes a problem.

- Work that has to pull the same fields out of the same material. If the result changes on every run, there is nothing to compare against.
- Testing and validation. What passed yesterday fails today.
- Tasks where several people need to receive the same result.

There are two ways to respond. On a developer connection, turn the randomness down as low as it goes and specify the same starting seed. Even then full reproducibility is not guaranteed, since computation order or a change on the service side can shake it.

The more reliable move is narrowing the output format. Pin the shape of the answer down to table cells, a fixed set of fields, or yes and no, and there is less room to diverge.

steps.title: The Limits of Next-Token Prediction
steps.contentMarkdown:
Knowing the structure also shows where the strengths and weaknesses divide.

**Sentence flow is strong.** Predicting what word comes next was drilled countless times, so natural prose comes out easily.

**Overall design is weak.** Since no conclusion is fixed at the outset, long pieces can lose their internal logic or forget a condition stated at the start. Asking for an outline first and then feeding that outline back in came out of this.

**One wrong turn gets built on.** Each new sentence rests on the ones before it, so a false premise early on ends up carrying everything after it. The model cannot back out on its own midway.

Hallucination, the subject of the next lesson, grows from the same root. Being a machine that continues a plausible next phrase rather than one that looks facts up is where the problem starts.

quiz.question: How does a generative model build an answer?
choices: It computes the entire answer in one pass and returns it
It scores the probability of the next token, picks one, appends it, and repeats
It retrieves the closest match from answers stored in advance
It builds the sentence backward, from the end to the beginning
quiz.explanation: The single calculation the model performs is scoring the probability of the next token. It picks one, appends it, and feeds the now longer text back in for the same calculation.

quiz.question: Which setting suits work that extracts fields from source material accurately?
choices: Raise the temperature to widen the range of candidates
Lower the temperature so weight concentrates on high-probability candidates
Change the temperature at random across several runs
The result is the same regardless of temperature
quiz.explanation: Lowering the temperature sharpens the distribution and stabilizes the output. That suits translation, summarizing, and data extraction, where accuracy matters.

quiz.question: Why does the internal logic of a long piece come apart so easily?
choices: Because long pieces were absent from the training material
Because it appends the next phrase as it goes instead of fixing a conclusion in advance
Because a cap on the number of sentences is in force
Because the spell checker is not running
quiz.explanation: The model appends one token after another rather than laying out an overall design first. Long pieces can therefore drop an earlier condition or drift out of logic, which is why asking for an outline first helps.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Why Hallucination Happens
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Sources and quotations that do not exist, delivered with confidence. Not a defect but a property of the structure.
objectives: Explain why hallucination arises from the generation structure
Recognize in advance the question types that invite hallucination
Set up a verification routine you can run as a user

steps.title: The Moment a Paper Gets Invented
steps.contentMarkdown:
A paper title, an author, and a year of publication come out in one line, and the paper does not exist. The format is flawless. The journal is real and the author is a real researcher. Only that combination is missing.

The same thing happens with court decisions, book page numbers, statistics, and interview quotes. This effect is called **hallucination**.

It is a different thing from a human lie. There is no intent to deceive, and on the model's side there is no awareness of having produced something that does not exist. It is the ordinary work of returning a plausibly formatted answer, carried out as usual.

Which means tone of voice gives nothing away. An accurate answer and an invented one arrive equally calm and equally confident. That is the most dangerous property of hallucination.
steps.imageAlt: A grand academic archive illusion revealed from the side as a thin painted stage flat with empty space behind it

steps.title: A Property of the Structure
steps.contentMarkdown:
The model is not a machine that looks facts up. It is a machine that computes the probability of what comes next.

After a phrase like according to a study published in 2019, a string shaped like a paper title has a high probability of following. The model produces a string that fits the slot. No step that checks whether the combination actually exists sits anywhere in the structure.

Facts are not stored inside the model as entries. They are dissolved across an enormous number of weights. Facts that appeared often are left dark and reproduce well. Facts that appeared rarely are left faint and blend with things that resemble them.

That is why the best known work of a famous figure comes out right while the fine details of a lesser known figure's career come out wrong. The boundary between what it knows and what it does not is not sharp, not even to the model itself.

steps.title: Questions That Invite Hallucination
steps.contentMarkdown:
Knowing these in advance makes defense easier. The risk climbs where the following overlap.

- **Asking for a specific identifier.** A paper title, a case number, a page number, an exact date, a quoted sentence.
- **Working on a topic with thin material.** Local figures, small organizations, one country's institutions, the details of an old event.
- **Asking it to find something that is not there.** Ask a question that presupposes a concept which does not exist and an explanation gets invented to fit the premise.
- **Asking about anything past the knowledge cutoff.** Rather than saying it does not know, the model sometimes continues as though it does.
- **Asking it to fill a long list.** Demand ten items and ten arrive even when only six have any basis.

The last one catches people especially often. Instead of pinning the count, attach a condition such as only the ones you have a basis for.

steps.title: What Search Removes and What It Leaves
steps.contentMarkdown:
Attaching search or document lookup cuts hallucination substantially, because the answer rests on material just read rather than on recall.

It does not all disappear.

- When the retrieved material is itself wrong. A bad blog post used as a source gets passed along as is.
- When the material gets summarized badly. Causal links absent from the original get added, or conditions get dropped.
- When source links are produced to match a format. Open them and the content is different, or the address does not exist.

So receiving sources is not the end of it. **The step of actually opening the link and confirming the sentence is in there** still remains. Skip that check and the benefit of attaching search is cut in half.

steps.title: Making Verification a Habit
steps.contentMarkdown:
This service applies the same rule to its own material. Anecdotes and quotations a model produces are accepted as data only after being checked independently against outside sources.

Four steps are worth keeping for everyday use.

- **Delegate only what you can verify.** Do not hand off fact-checking in a field where you cannot confirm the answer yourself.
- **Confirm identifiers at the original.** Titles, years, page numbers, and case numbers get read directly from the source material.
- **Ask differently and watch for wobble.** Put the same question again in different words. An answer that shifts is a sign the basis is thin.
- **State up front that not knowing is an acceptable answer.** Push back on the tendency to fill gaps at the request stage.

Hallucination is not a defect you can switch off in the settings. It is more accurate to treat these systems as tools you use with a verification step attached alongside.

quiz.question: What is the underlying reason hallucination occurs?
choices: False information is mixed into the training material
The structure continues a plausible next phrase with no step that looks facts up
It only happens when the internet connection drops
The user asked a difficult question
quiz.explanation: The model is not a fact lookup system but one that computes the probability of the next token. It produces a string that fits the slot, and no step confirming that the thing exists sits in the structure.

quiz.question: Which request carries the highest risk of hallucination?
choices: Asking for an explanation of a widely known concept
Asking for a sentence to be tightened up
Asking for exactly ten accurate references on a little known topic
Asking for the spelling in a piece of writing to be fixed
quiz.explanation: Risk peaks where thin material, specific identifiers, and a pinned item count overlap. The model tends to fill the count even when the basis runs short.

quiz.question: What check still remains even for an answer produced with search attached?
choices: Ask for the answer again at greater length
Open the cited links directly and confirm the content is there
Repeat the same question ten times
Translate the answer into another language
quiz.explanation: Retrieved material can be wrong, a summary can drift from the original, and a link can be formatted correctly but lead nowhere. Skipping the step of opening the source cuts the benefit of search.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Where the Tone Comes From
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Pretraining, fine-tuning, preference tuning. Why models that start from the same base end up with a different character in every service.
objectives: Distinguish what each of the three training stages installs
Explain why the same base model ends up with different characters
Recognize the side effects that the alignment process leaves behind

steps.title: Training Split Into Three Stages
steps.contentMarkdown:
The conversational models in use today are not built in a single round of training. They pass through stages of quite different character, one after another.

| Stage | What it does | What it installs |
|---|---|---|
| Pretraining | Predict the next token across vast amounts of text | Feel for language, knowledge of the world |
| Fine-tuning | Learn from pairs of instructions and model answers | The shape of following a request |
| Preference tuning | Fold in preferences chosen by people | Tone, refusal thresholds, safety judgment |

Cost and time are overwhelmingly concentrated in the first stage. The two that follow are comparatively small. Yet the character a user perceives is settled almost entirely in those two.

That building the bulk and setting the character are separate jobs is the core of this structure.
steps.imageAlt: One pottery workshop arranged continuously from basic forming to functional refinement to selection of the finished vessel

steps.title: Pretraining: Acquiring a Feel for Language
steps.contentMarkdown:
Enormous quantities of text go in, including web pages, books, encyclopedias, and code, and the model is trained to predict the next token. No person has to label anything. The text already contains the answer in the form of the word that comes next.

A model that finishes this stage continues sentences remarkably well. It is hard to use as a conversation partner. Ask it a question and instead of answering it may generate more questions like yours, because on the open internet a question is often followed by another question.

Knowledge enters at this stage too. What appeared often is left dark, what appeared rarely is left faint. The knowledge cutoff is set here as well.

Bulk and knowledge in place but not in usable shape: that is a base model with pretraining finished.

steps.title: Fine-tuning: Into the Shape of Following a Request
steps.contentMarkdown:
The next stage feeds in material that pairs instructions with model answers. Large numbers of examples show that asking this way gets answered that way.

After this the character changes sharply. It answers questions, follows requirements about format, and breaks explanations into steps. Knowledge does not increase much. What changes is closer to how the existing knowledge gets brought out.

This is also where models diverge by purpose. Layer legal documents onto a given base model and legal phrasing comes out. Layer support transcripts on and a support tone comes out. This is the method companies use to build internal models.

It is the same reason several services with entirely different characters can come from one public base model. The foundation is identical and the material layered on top differs.

steps.title: Preference Tuning: Setting the Tone and the Refusal Line
steps.contentMarkdown:
Finally, human preferences get folded in. People compare several answers to the same question, pick the better one, and that judgment goes into training.

This is where the character of each service hardens.

- Tone. Stiff or warm, long explanations or short ones.
- Refusal thresholds. How far it answers and where it stops.
- Posture under uncertainty. Whether it asserts or says it does not know.
- Format habits. Whether it reaches for lists or writes in paragraphs.

The criteria for choosing preferences are set by the company. Its judgment about which answer is better is its policy, and that policy hardens into the character of the model.

Ask the same question of several services and the content is often similar while the manner differs. Usually that gap comes from this stage.

steps.title: Side Effects That Alignment Leaves
steps.contentMarkdown:
Folding in human preference grows some branches nobody planted, because what people rate more highly does not always line up with what is accurate.

**It leans toward agreeing.** When a user pushes a false premise, a tendency emerges to go along rather than push back. That is the trace of human raters generally rating agreeable answers higher.

**It is excessively cautious.** Harmless requests get refused, or so many qualifications get attached that the answer itself blurs.

**It treats long, formal answers as good.** Questions that could end in one line arrive with lists and subheadings.

The response is to pin things down at the request stage. Ask for the opposing view, ask for a stated level of confidence, specify the length. Knowing which defaults are installed is what lets you write a request that strips those defaults away.

The next course covers how to write that request.

quiz.question: What state is a base model in after pretraining finishes?
choices: Ready to use as a conversation partner that answers questions directly
Good at continuing sentences but not in the shape of answering a request
Without knowledge but already in conversational form
Fully finished, with human preferences already folded in
quiz.explanation: Pretraining installs a feel for language and knowledge through next-token prediction. The shape of answering a request appears in the next stage, fine-tuning.

quiz.question: Why do services with entirely different characters come out of the same base model?
choices: Because pretraining is redone from scratch for each service
Because the material layered on and the criteria used differ at the fine-tuning and preference tuning stages
Because each service splits text into tokens differently
Because the servers sit in different locations
quiz.explanation: Expensive pretraining builds the foundation, and character is settled in the two later stages. Different layered material and different preference criteria yield different characters from the same foundation.

quiz.question: What side effect comes out of folding in human preferences?
choices: Knowledge disappears
Sentences stop being grammatical
It leans toward agreeing with the user and answers run longer than needed
It loses the ability to handle other languages
quiz.explanation: The answer people rate highly and the accurate answer do not always coincide. An agreeable posture, excessive caution, and long formal formatting are left behind as defaults.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: The Four Slots of a Prompt
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Context, task, format, constraints. Filling those four slots is what separates a usable result from a generic one.
objectives: Tell the four parts of a prompt apart and write each one down
Predict how the same task changes when it is asked two different ways
Spot the missing slot and rewrite the prompt around it

steps.title: A thin request gets a thin answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
Type `Write a blog post` and you get something serviceable. Serviceable means it fits nobody in particular.

The model fills every gap with a guess. No reader given, so it assumes an average reader. No length given, so it picks something in the middle. Stack up enough guesses and the output settles into the average.

Try again.

`This is a science blog for middle school students. Explain photosynthesis in about 400 words. Use three subheadings and exactly one analogy. Do not use chemical formulas.`

Same task, completely different result. Reader, length, structure, and prohibitions are all fixed now. Writing a good prompt is not a hunt for clever phrasing. It is **filling in the information you left out**.

steps.title: A four slot checklist
steps.contentMarkdown:
Keeping the parts of a prompt in four slots saves you from starting from nothing every time.

| Slot | What goes in it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Context | Who reads it, why, what the situation is | Science blog for middle schoolers, classroom handout |
| Task | Exactly what you want done | Write an explanation of how photosynthesis works |
| Format | The shape you want it back in | 400 words, three subheadings, prose |
| Constraints | What to avoid, what to hold to | No chemical formulas, one analogy only |

You do not have to fill all four. A short question needs the task and nothing else. The value shows up when a result disappoints: look back at which slot was empty and the fix is already visible.

In practice the slot left empty most often is context. The situation is sitting in your head, so you skip writing it down.
steps.imageAlt: An overhead fabrication bench physically integrating user, task, finished shell, and height limit in one child-scale sluice exhibit

steps.title: Context means reader and purpose
steps.contentMarkdown:
Two things belong in the context slot. Who reads it, and what it gets used for.

The same topic turns into different writing when the reader changes. `An investment analyst will read this` and `A student meeting the topic for the first time will read this` pull different vocabulary and different depth.

Write the purpose as well. Say `This opens a presentation` and the first sentence comes out built to hold an audience. Say `This is an internal memo` and the conclusion moves to the front.

Assigning a role is common too, as in `You are an editor with twenty years of experience`. It sometimes helps, but keep expectations modest. No knowledge appears that was not already there. Tone and point of view tilt that way, and that is the whole effect.

Naming the reader and the purpose moves the result far more reliably than naming a role.

steps.title: Pin the task down with a verb
steps.contentMarkdown:
One mistake shows up in the task slot over and over. You write the topic and never say what to do with it.

Type `about remote work` and there is no telling whether you get an overview or a list of arguments for and against. The verb has to be pinned down.

- `List three advantages and three disadvantages of adopting remote work`
- `Rebut the arguments against adopting remote work`
- `Draft a remote work policy as numbered clauses`

Three requests, three unrelated deliverables. The task slot is where you decide which job this is: summarize, compare, draft, review, classify, translate, extract.

Avoid stacking several tasks into one request. Ask for a summary plus a critique plus an alternative in one shot and all three come out shallow. Split them.

steps.title: Constraints protect the result
steps.contentMarkdown:
The constraint slot is the easiest one to leave blank and it pays off more than the rest. Writing down what to avoid cuts the cleanup afterward.

Collect the constraints you reach for often and reuse them.

- `Leave out anything you cannot support, and write that you do not know when you do not`
- `When you include a number or a quotation, name its source alongside it`
- `Write in prose paragraphs only, with no subheadings and no lists`
- `No inflated modifiers and no encouraging line at the end`
- `Add nothing that is not in the source text`

As the earlier course showed, training left the model with a habit of treating long, formal answers as better ones. Stripping that default off takes direct pressure inside the prompt.

Build the constraint list that matches your own work once and you can attach it to every prompt after that. The next lesson looks at how long a prompt can get and where the ceiling sits.

quiz.question: Which one is not one of the four slots of a prompt?
choices: Context
Task
Model name
Constraints
quiz.explanation: The four slots are context, task, format, and constraints. Which model you happen to be using is not something you write inside the prompt.

quiz.question: What belongs in the context slot?
choices: Who reads it and what it will be used for
The character count of the answer
A list of expressions to avoid
How many times to repeat the request
quiz.explanation: Context is reader and purpose. Stating who reads it and what it is for moves the result more reliably than assigning a role.

quiz.question: What happens when one request asks for a summary, a critique, and an alternative together?
choices: All three come out more accurate
All three come out shallow, so splitting them into separate requests works better
Only the summary is produced and the rest is ignored
The request gets refused
quiz.explanation: Overlapping tasks split the attention and the space each one gets, so all three end up thin. Ask for them separately.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: How Much It Can Read at Once
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Long conversations blur what came first. Once you know the context window has a ceiling, you have a rule for splitting long work.
objectives: Understand what the context window is and what sits inside it
Learn how to feed a long document in piece by piece
Judge when to move to a fresh conversation

steps.title: As much as fits on the desk
steps.contentMarkdown:
The range a model consults while producing an answer is fixed. That range is the **context window**, and its size is measured in tokens.

A desk is a useful picture. The model answers from whatever is spread out on the desk. Anything left in a drawer is invisible. A small desk cannot hold every document at once.

What sits in the context window is more than the question you typed.

- Instructions the service inserted ahead of you
- The entire conversation so far
- Text you pasted and the contents of attached files
- Material pulled in by search
- The answer being generated right now

All of it has to fit under the ceiling together. Window sizes differ by service and by model and they keep growing year over year, but at any given moment a ceiling exists.
steps.imageAlt: An archivist able to examine only the records on a small circular light table while the rest remain in closed cabinets

steps.title: What happens when the ceiling is passed
steps.contentMarkdown:
Keep a long conversation going and a moment arrives when the rules you set at the start stop holding. You asked for a different tone and the old one comes back. A phrase you banned reappears.

Past the ceiling, the front of the conversation usually gets cut away. Some services do this quietly, without telling you. Once it is cut, that content might as well never have existed.

Trouble shows up under the ceiling too. Several experiments report that information sitting in the middle of a long context gets missed. The beginning and the end hold up while the middle blurs.

So conditions that absolutely must hold go at the front or the back of the request. When you paste in long material, put the material first and the instructions last.

steps.title: How to feed in a long document
steps.contentMarkdown:
Dumping the whole document in is not always the best move. Cost goes up and accuracy can go down.

- **Excerpt it.** Feed only the sections that matter. You can paste the table of contents first and have the model pick which sections those are.
- **Split the work.** Get a summary per chapter, then feed those summaries back in to reach an overall conclusion.
- **Mark the structure.** Put a divider before and after the material so it is clear where the source starts and stops. This keeps source text and instructions from bleeding into each other.
- **Forbid going outside the source.** Attach `Do not include anything that is not in the material below`.

That last item carries weight. Without it, background knowledge that is nowhere in the document gets mixed in, and reviewing the document stops meaning anything at all.

steps.title: When to move to a new conversation
steps.contentMarkdown:
Continuing the same conversation is not always the better choice. There are signals that it is time to move.

- The rules you set at the start keep getting broken.
- You have raised the same point twice or more and nothing has changed.
- The topic has drifted somewhere other than where you started.
- Several failed attempts have piled up in the conversation.

That last signal matters most. Wrong attempts left in the context keep pulling the work in their direction. With three bad drafts sitting above it, the fourth comes out looking much the same.

When you move, carry over only the conclusions that are settled. Asking for a summary first makes them easy to move. People often spend more time protecting a conversation than starting a clean one would have cost.

steps.title: Memory features are not a wider window
steps.contentMarkdown:
It is easy to read a service memory feature as the context window having grown. It has not.

A memory feature stores what you said somewhere else and pastes it back at the top when a new conversation starts. From the model side it is context being read fresh again, and it occupies the context window in proportion to how much got pasted.

So as stored memories accumulate, the room left for the work in front of you shrinks. Old memories also cut into current work and get in the way.

Put plainly: the inside of the model does not change through conversation. What changes is what gets read back to it. Deciding what to keep and what to clear is your job.

quiz.question: Which one does not sit inside the context window?
choices: The conversation up to this point
The body text of a document you pasted
The entire original training corpus
The answer being generated right now
quiz.explanation: Instructions, the conversation, pasted material, search results, and the answer in progress all share the context window. Training data is dissolved inside the model and never loaded into that window.

quiz.question: Why should conditions that must hold go at the front or the back of a request?
choices: Sentences at the edges are cheaper to process
Information placed in the middle of a long context is reported to get missed
There is a character limit that applies to the middle
Position makes no difference, so it is only a habit
quiz.explanation: Even under the ceiling, the middle of a long context blurs, and that has been observed across several experiments. Key conditions belong at one end or the other.

quiz.question: In a conversation where several failed attempts have piled up, what is worth doing?
choices: Repeat the same request in stronger language
Carry only the settled conclusions into a fresh conversation
Ask it to delete the front of the conversation
Ask for a longer answer and try again
quiz.explanation: Wrong attempts left in the context keep pulling the work their way. Summarizing the conclusions and moving them into a new conversation is faster.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: An Example Beats an Explanation
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Showing the shape you want once saves ten lines of description. Here is how to pin a format down.
objectives: Understand how examples are supplied and what they do
Fix the output by specifying the format up front
Recognize the cases where examples backfire

steps.title: The part that resists description
steps.contentMarkdown:
Try describing the tone you want in words and you stall almost immediately. What comes out is `Not too stiff, but not too breezy either, just plain`. A person could not work from that description either.

One example solves it. Paste a paragraph you like and write `Match this tone`. Word choice, sentence length, and the way sentences close all transfer at once.

Supplying examples inside the request is called few-shot prompting. It is not training. It happens inside the request, so the model itself does not change, and the imitation lasts only for that conversation.

Tone, table shape, classification criteria, the way material gets organized: anything **awkward to put into words** is faster to hand over as an example.
steps.imageAlt: A woodworking apprentice building a new stool frame to match the proportions of one finished asymmetric wooden stool

steps.title: How to supply examples
steps.contentMarkdown:
An example pairs an input with an output.

Write `Sort each item into the format below.` and attach one pair. `Input: review of the iPhone 15 / Output: product=iPhone 15, category=electronics, sentiment=positive`

A few pointers.

- **Two or three is enough.** More of them eat the context window and still leave cases the examples never covered.
- **Pick different kinds.** Two examples that differ in character beat three that look alike. One positive and one negative, say.
- **Include an awkward case.** Show how an ambiguous input gets handled and that judgment carries over with it.
- **The examples themselves have to be right.** An error inside an example gets adopted as a rule.

steps.title: Pinning the format cuts the cleanup
steps.contentMarkdown:
Leave the format open and you get a different shape every time. Subheadings appear and vanish, lists turn back into paragraphs. Given the sampling step covered in the earlier course, that is exactly what you should expect.

Pinning the format down is straightforward.

- **Specify the shape.** `Lay this out as a table with three columns: item, evidence, risk.`
- **Specify the length.** `Keep every entry to two sentences or fewer.`
- **Specify the headers.** `Start each entry with a bold one line heading.`
- **Ban the preamble.** `Output the result only, with no explanation and no greeting.`

If a program consumes the output, format specification is not optional. One wobble in the structure and everything downstream breaks. Attaching a single format example is far steadier here than describing it.

steps.title: When examples work against you
steps.contentMarkdown:
Examples act with force. Supply the wrong ones and they push the result off course with the same force.

**Examples that lean one way.** Three positive cases and nothing else, and a negative case arriving later gets tilted toward positive as well.

**Wording that gets copied.** Specific phrases from the tone example turn up verbatim in the output. Stating the scope reduces it. `Do not reuse the wording. Take only the sentence length and the tone.`

**Format squeezing the content.** You asked for a table and material that does not fit a table gets forced into cells anyway. Leave one open column, or allow a note outside the table.

If a result resembles the examples too closely, cut the number of examples or swap them for ones with a different character.

steps.title: Keeping a working set on hand
steps.contentMarkdown:
If you repeat the same kind of work, keep the examples and formats somewhere separate. It is faster than rebuilding them each time and the results come out more even.

Three things are worth keeping.

- Two or three paragraphs that show your own voice clearly
- A few output formats you use often
- The constraint list you attach every time

This project runs the same way. Every repeated job has a specification document, and the document gets read at the start of the work. Instead of a person remembering the rules and retyping them, the document holds them.

One caution. Examples go stale. If your voice has moved on and old examples are still attached, old results come back. When output starts feeling off, suspect the examples first.

quiz.question: What effect does few-shot prompting have on the model?
choices: The model learns the examples and keeps them permanently
They are consulted only inside that request and conversation, and the model itself does not change
The model's knowledge cutoff moves forward
Other users see the effect in their results too
quiz.explanation: Putting examples inside a request is not training. They are imitated within that context and nothing remains once the conversation ends.

quiz.question: What is the better way to choose examples?
choices: Include ten or more examples that resemble each other
Pick two or three that differ in character and include an awkward case
Include one easy example and nothing more
Skip examples and write a long description instead
quiz.explanation: Two or three cover it, and pairing different kinds with an ambiguous case is what communicates the criteria.

quiz.question: The wording from your tone example keeps appearing in the output. What do you do?
choices: Add more examples
State the scope: do not reuse the wording, take only sentence length and tone
Remove every format instruction
Ask for a longer answer
quiz.explanation: Examples act with force, so wording gets copied along with tone. Name the scope to borrow from, or swap in an example with a different character.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Make It Work in Steps
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Demand a conclusion in one move and steps get skipped. Specifying an order and inserting checkpoints raises accuracy.
objectives: Understand how to split a request into steps and why it helps
Build a routine that reviews the plan before the work
Separate the tasks that need steps from the ones that do not

steps.title: Ask for the conclusion first and steps get skipped
steps.contentMarkdown:
A generative model builds an answer by appending one token after another. Once it starts writing a conclusion, everything after it gets filled in to support that conclusion. A conclusion reached without checking does not get walked back on its own later.

Questions with arithmetic or comparison in them expose this. Ask for a direct answer to a problem carrying three conditions and one condition drops out. The answer still looks flawless in form.

Specifying an order changes the outcome. `Check each condition one at a time, then write your conclusion.` Once the checking is written out first, that text is read back as context while the conclusion forms.

You are making room to think before the answer. Research has confirmed that this works, and services now often handle the process internally.

steps.title: How to specify an order
steps.contentMarkdown:
Break the work into steps and number them.

`Work in this order. 1) Pull and quote every relevant clause from the source. 2) Judge clause by clause whether it applies to our situation. 3) Collect only the ones that apply and write the action each requires.`

Written this way, extraction and judgment do not blend into each other. Tracing an error afterward gets easier too. If step three looks wrong, go check the quotations in step one.

A few rules for splitting steps.

- **One job per step.** Ask it to judge while extracting and the two mix.
- **Make later steps consume earlier results.** Listing unrelated steps accomplishes nothing.
- **Ask to see the intermediate results.** Hidden work cannot be checked.

steps.title: Get the plan first
steps.contentMarkdown:
On anything sizable, taking the plan before the deliverable is safer.

`Do not write it yet. Give me the outline and what each section will cover. I will review that before you write the body.`

Catch a wrong direction at the plan stage and a few lines of correction settle it. Catch it after the full text arrives and the whole thing gets rewritten.

The review points are fixed as well. Is the scope right, is anything missing, does the order follow naturally. Those three catch most of the drift.

When you correct a plan, have the corrected plan written out again. Pointing something out in passing sometimes never reaches the body. The revised plan has to exist as text in the context for the work that follows to obey it.
steps.imageAlt: An engineer checking the joint sequence on a scale bridge model before work begins across the real empty span

steps.title: Make it review its own work
steps.contentMarkdown:
Requesting a review as a separate step after the result arrives does catch things.

`Mark the claims in the answer above that rest on weak support.`
`Pull only the sentences in the draft above that need fact checking.`
`Argue against this conclusion from the opposing position.`

Asked as a follow up in the same conversation, the previous answer is sitting in the context, so that is what gets reviewed. Finding faults in your own output has limits, but it beats no review at all.

One caution. Ask in a doubting tone, as in `Is that actually right?`, and correct answers get changed too. That is the agreeable tilt the earlier course covered.

When you ask for a review, name the criteria to review against. Presence of support, whether conditions are met, whether a claim needs fact checking.

steps.title: When steps are not worth it
steps.contentMarkdown:
Not every request needs steps attached. Splitting work adds cost and time.

Steps are worth it here.

- Judgments carrying several conditions
- Work that extracts from a source, organizes it, and then reaches a conclusion
- Anything mixing calculation and comparison
- Long deliverables where structure matters

And clearly not worth it here.

- Translation, spelling correction, tone polishing
- Short fact checks
- Format conversion

Attach steps to that second group and the preamble grows while the actual result stays the same. Better to put `Output the result only, with no explanation` into the constraint slot from the earlier lesson.

There is one test. Would a person doing this job need scratch notes along the way. If yes, make room for them.

quiz.question: Why is a request that demands the conclusion straight away a disadvantage?
choices: The answer comes out shorter
Once a conclusion is started, what follows gets written to support it, and the model cannot walk itself back
It costs more to run
The formatting falls apart
quiz.explanation: The model extends what it has already written. A conclusion produced without checking will not be reversed later, so put the checking in front of it.

quiz.question: Why take the plan first on a sizable piece of work?
choices: Plans are more accurate than bodies of text
A wrong direction can be corrected in a few lines
Plans cost nothing to produce
You no longer have to write the body
quiz.explanation: Drift found after the full text arrives means rewriting the whole thing. Caught at the plan stage, the cost of correction is far smaller.

quiz.question: Which task does not need to be split into steps?
choices: A judgment carrying several conditions
Extracting items from a source, organizing them, and reaching a conclusion
Correcting the spelling in a sentence
A review that mixes calculation and comparison
quiz.explanation: Work a person handles without scratch notes has no use for steps. Spelling correction and format conversion just gain a longer preamble.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Do Not Try to Finish in One Pass
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: The first result is a draft. Naming where and how to change it is what lifts the quality.
objectives: Learn to request partial edits instead of a full rewrite
Use wording that locks down the parts you liked
Judge when to stop revising and start clean

steps.title: Treat the first result as a draft
steps.contentMarkdown:
Expect a finished piece from a single request and you will be disappointed. When you hand work to a person you get a draft and shape it together. Nothing changes here.

What the first result gives you is not polish, it is **information**. It shows how your request was read. A result pointed the wrong way means the prompt had an empty slot.

Three things to check when the first result lands.

- Was the task understood correctly
- Did the format come out as asked
- Do the facts and the supporting evidence hold

If the first one is off, fix the prompt and start over. If only the second and third are off, keep going and revise from here.

steps.title: Do not ask for a rewrite
steps.contentMarkdown:
`Rewrite it` is the most expensive request you can make. The parts that came out well disappear along with everything else, and because of the sampling step you get something entirely different. The second paragraph you liked may never come back.

Name the spot to change instead.

`Drop the statistic in the second paragraph and put one concrete case there instead. Leave the rest as it is.`
`The last sentence preaches. Turn it into plain description.`
`The third and fifth items say the same thing. Merge them.`

The more specific the target, the more of the surrounding text survives. If the position is hard to describe, quote the sentence you want changed. Then there is no room to misread which sentence you meant.
steps.imageAlt: A conservator repairing only one small tear in an otherwise intact tapestry

steps.title: Lock down what should stay
steps.contentMarkdown:
Things you never asked about get changed all the time. Touch one spot and the tone of the neighboring sentence shifts with it.

Naming what to preserve reduces that.
