`Leave the first and last paragraphs exactly as they are.`
`Keep the title and the subheadings.`
`Keep the overall length close to what it is now.`

After several rounds the original requirements start to fade as well. Restating the conditions so far after about three exchanges brings things back into line.

On a large deliverable there is another option: take back only a piece. `Rewrite the third section only. Do not print the rest.` That narrows the editable surface physically rather than by instruction.

steps.title: Take several and choose
steps.contentMarkdown:
There is a route other than revising. Take several results from the start and pick one.

`Give me ten title candidates. Spread them across different directions.` Out of a batch like that, one is usually usable, or two can be combined.

This suits work where the direction is still open. Titles, openings, structural approaches, and naming are the usual cases.

One caution. Ask for ten with nothing else and you get ten similar things, because candidates already written sit in the context and pull the later ones toward them. Write `in different directions`, or divide the directions up front. `Three each in explanatory, question, and quotation form.`

Once the direction is settled, lifting one candidate beats generating more of them.

steps.title: When to stop and start clean
steps.contentMarkdown:
Continuing to revise is not always the winning move.

Raise the same point three times with nothing changing and stop. Failed attempts have accumulated in the context and the work is being pulled along by them. This is the moment for the conversation switch from the earlier lesson.

When you start clean, take what you have earned with you.

- Turn the settled requirements into a list
- Attach the paragraphs you liked as examples
- Write the failed directions into the do not list

The third one matters. Without a record of what did not work, the new conversation falls into the same hole.

And if the deliverable is nearly there, finishing the rest by hand is often quicker. At some point the round trips needed to delegate the final polish cost more than doing it yourself.

quiz.question: Why is `Rewrite it` an expensive request?
choices: It costs twice as much to run
The parts that came out well are lost too, and the result can come back completely different
The exact same result repeats
Format instructions stop applying
quiz.explanation: A full rewrite throws away the parts you wanted to keep. Because candidates are sampled, what you liked may not come back at all.

quiz.question: How do you reduce changes to parts you never asked about?
choices: Ask for a longer answer
Name what should stay untouched, or narrow the range to be rewritten
Send the same request twice
Remove the format instructions
quiz.explanation: Stating what not to touch, or asking for one section only, leaves far less room for the rest to shift.

quiz.question: What must you carry into a new conversation?
choices: The complete transcript of the previous conversation
The settled requirements plus a record of what failed
The configuration values of the model you used
The timestamps of your requests
quiz.explanation: Without a record of the failed directions, the new conversation falls into the same hole. Move the settled conditions, the examples you liked, and the failure list together.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: The Habit of Checking Answers
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: A routine for catching confident wrong answers, and a rule for deciding what to delegate and what to keep.
objectives: Set up a routine that asks for sources and actually checks them
Learn how to test whether an answer wobbles
Separate work you can delegate from work you cannot

steps.title: Tone tells you nothing
steps.contentMarkdown:
An accurate answer and an invented one arrive in the same voice. As the earlier course showed, there is no awareness inside the structure that something was fabricated, so there is no reason for the manner to differ.

Verification therefore has to be a routine, not a feeling. Checking only the parts that look odd fails. The passage written most convincingly can be the invented one.

The items that need checking are a fixed set.

- Names of people, names of organizations, titles of works
- Years, dates, figures, percentages
- Quoted sentences and their sources
- Statutes, regulations, court decisions
- Links and document titles

Description and explanation are relatively safe. Picking out only what falls on that list cuts the burden sharply.
steps.imageAlt: A surveyor checking two equally convincing unmarked compasses against a noon meridian shadow

steps.title: How to ask for sources
steps.contentMarkdown:
Ask for sources and nothing more, and you may get something that only satisfies the form. Make the demand concrete.

`After each claim, give the document name and the specific passage it rests on. Mark any claim you cannot support as no source found.`

That last sentence is the load bearing one. Without a place to record the absence, the blank gets filled. It is the same property as the list filling covered in the earlier course.

In an environment with search attached, take the links along with the claims. Then work remains. **Open the link and see whether that sentence is actually there.** Confirming the title and moving on is not checking.

If the source is paywalled or otherwise out of reach, leave that item unverified. Passing off something unchecked as checked empties the whole routine of meaning.

steps.title: Ask differently and watch for wobble
steps.contentMarkdown:
Throw the same question back with different wording and you get a sense of how thick the supporting evidence is.

A fact with solid support gives the same answer however you ask. A thin one shifts with the phrasing. The year changes, or the person does.

A few pointers.

- Ask in a new conversation. Asked in the same one, the earlier answer sits in the context and gets repeated.
- Reverse the framing. Instead of `Is it true that A did B?`, ask `What is actually established about the relationship between A and B?`
- Slip in something that never happened. If an invented premise is accepted and explained anyway, the evidence on that topic is thin.

Stability is not correctness, though. A widely circulated error is wrong consistently. The wobble test does not replace going to the source.

steps.title: Decide what not to delegate
steps.contentMarkdown:
Judgments in a field you cannot verify are better not delegated at all. If you cannot tell whether the result is right, there is no verification routine to speak of.

Splitting the work into two columns looks like this.

| Safe to delegate | Handle with care |
|---|---|
| Drafting, tightening the wording | Work where one fact decides the conclusion |
| Format conversion, classification, organizing | Legal, medical, and tax judgments |
| Translation drafts | Final conclusions in a field you cannot check |
| Widening the range of ideas | Final confirmation of a calculation |

The right column is not off limits. Use it for drafts and review lists, and move the final call to a person or a specialist.

One line makes the test easy. **Who answers for it when it is wrong.** If the answer is you, attach a verification routine.

steps.title: Put verification into the prompt
steps.contentMarkdown:
Building the checks in as conditions from the start is less work than auditing afterward.

- `Mark anything you are not certain of as needs checking`
- `Write that you do not know when you do not, and do not fill gaps with guesses`
- `Give a confidence level of high, medium, or low for every item`
- `Do not add unsupported items to reach a target count`
- `Do not include anything that is not in the material below`

The confidence level is especially useful. It tells you what to check first. Keep in mind that the label itself was produced by the model and carries no guarantee. Start with the low ones, but do not wave the high ones through.

This project handles its own material the same way. Anecdotes and quotations about a person are never taken as the model produced them. They become project data only after an independent cross check.

quiz.question: Which items should be verified first?
choices: General conceptual explanations
Names, years, figures, quotations, and their sources
The tone of the sentences
The overall length of the answer
quiz.explanation: Description and explanation are relatively safe. Concrete identifiers such as names, dates, figures, quotations, and statutes are what you check.

quiz.question: What condition is worth adding when you ask for sources?
choices: List as many sources as possible
Mark any claim you cannot support as no source found
Present sources in English only
Collect all sources at the very end of the answer
quiz.explanation: Without somewhere to record an absence, the blank gets filled. Leaving open the option to write no source found is the point.

quiz.question: You asked the same question in different ways and the answer did not wobble. What does that mean?
choices: It can be treated as established fact
You can skip going to the source
The support may well be thick, but widely circulated errors are wrong consistently, so the source still needs checking
The topic cannot be verified at all
quiz.explanation: The wobble test is a rough gauge of how thick the evidence is. Widely circulated errors stay wrong consistently, so it cannot replace going to the source.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: AI With Search and Tools Attached
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Answering from memory and answering after reading fetched material are two different things. You need to know which one you are getting.
objectives: Distinguish internal model knowledge from external retrieval
Identify what still needs checking in a search backed answer
Set a rule for handing calculation, current facts, and document lookup to tools

steps.title: Two routes to an answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
The same question can travel two routes.

**Answering from memory.** What dissolved into the weights during training gets pulled out. Fast and cheap. Bound to the knowledge cutoff, unable to cite anything, and unreliable on rare facts.

**Fetching, reading, then answering.** The question triggers a search across the web or a document set, the material comes back, and the answer is formed with that material in the context. Slower and more expensive. Handles current facts and can point at evidence.

The second approach is retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. For internal policies, product documentation, and paper collections that the model never learned, it has become the standard structure.

The first thing to establish is which route the window in front of you takes. Whether evidence links appear and whether a search indicator shows up usually settles it.

steps.title: The weak links in a retrieval answer
steps.contentMarkdown:
Attached evidence is not grounds for relaxing. This structure has several stages and any of them can go wrong.

- **The fetching stage.** Pull in unrelated material and the answer gets built on top of it. Badly chosen search terms are a common cause.
- **The material itself.** What came back may be wrong or out of date. Superseded regulations, sloppy summaries, promotional pages.
- **The reading stage.** Causal links absent from the source get added, or a qualifying clause gets dropped.
- **The citing stage.** The link points at A while the content came from B.

The fourth is the hardest to catch. A plausible link title invites you to move on without opening it.

The check collapses into one action. Open the link and look for the sentence.

steps.title: Requests that make it use the tools
steps.contentMarkdown:
Even with tools attached, it sometimes answers from memory instead of using them. Saying so in the request changes that.

`Search and confirm before answering. Include the evidence links.`
`Do not calculate this yourself. Run code and give me the result.`
`Answer only from the attached document. If it is not in there, say so.`

Which tools are available differs by service. The common ones are web search, code execution, document lookup, and image generation.

Pushing calculation into code helps the most. As the earlier course showed, long numbers get split into tokens and place value gets scrambled, and running code sidesteps that entirely. Table totals, date arithmetic, and unit conversion are safer handed to code.

steps.title: When you supply the material yourself
steps.contentMarkdown:
Sometimes pasting the material in yourself is more reliable than leaving it to search, because you control which material the answer rests on.

A few things to hold to.

- **Mark the boundaries of the material.** Make it clear where the source starts and stops. This prevents sentences inside the source from being read as instructions.
- **Forbid going outside the material.** Mixing in background knowledge empties the review of meaning.
- **Require citation.** Have it note which part of the material each judgment rests on.
- **Cut the volume.** Feeding only the relevant sections raises accuracy and lowers cost.

Documents from outside carry one more risk. If a sentence inside the document looks like an instruction, the model may try to follow it. When you feed in a document from a source you do not trust, do not execute the output as it stands.

steps.title: How much to leave automatic
steps.contentMarkdown:
As the range of tools widens, so does the number of actions no person reviewed. Some setups do not stop at fetching and reading; they go on to edit files, send mail, or place orders.

Sorting by reversibility makes the call easy.

- **Reversible work.** Drafting, looking things up, calculating, reading files. Delegate it and review the result.
- **Hard to reverse.** Sending, paying, deleting, publishing, sharing outside. A person checks before it runs.

Writing the checkpoint into the prompt is another approach. `Show me the draft and get my approval before sending anything.`

This lands in the same place as the verification test from the earlier lesson. When the consequence of being wrong comes back to you, a person holds the last step.
steps.imageAlt: A worker inspecting the first unmarked CNC part with a caliper while holding the batch-start lever

quiz.question: How does retrieval augmented generation differ from answering from memory?
choices: It updates the values inside the model as it goes
It fetches material, places it in the context, and answers on that basis
The knowledge cutoff disappears
Hallucination is eliminated completely
quiz.explanation: Retrieval augmented generation does not modify the model. It fetches material into the context and forms the answer on top of that material.

quiz.question: Why is handing table totals or date arithmetic to code execution safer?
choices: Code runs faster
It sidesteps the problem of numbers being split into tokens and place value getting scrambled
Code execution is free
It stores the results of the calculation
quiz.explanation: Long numbers get split across several tokens and place value gets scrambled. Moving the calculation itself into code avoids that weakness.

quiz.question: Which kind of work is risky to leave automatic without human review?
choices: Looking up material
Producing a draft
Hard to reverse actions such as sending mail or making a payment
Reading a file
quiz.explanation: Reversible work can be delegated, but actions that are hard to undo, such as sending, paying, deleting, or publishing, run only after a person checks them.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Five Common Failures
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: The tilt toward agreement, dropped instructions, unsupported confidence. Recognize the symptoms and prepare the response in advance.
objectives: Recognize the recurring failure types and their symptoms
Build the matching response into your prompts
Trace failures back to conditions on your own side

steps.title: It tilts toward agreeing with you
steps.contentMarkdown:
Push a false premise and it sometimes builds an explanation on top of it rather than pushing back. Give it a correct answer, then ask `Are you sure about that?`, and the answer can change.

As the earlier course showed, this was planted at the stage that folds in human preference. Raters generally scored agreeable answers higher, and the trace remains.

The symptoms look like this. Every time you point something out it apologizes and revises, yet accuracy does not improve. Ask about two opposing claims separately and it agrees with both.

The response is to change how you ask.

- `If my reasoning is wrong, point out exactly where`
- `Find evidence that argues against this conclusion`
- Ask neutrally, without revealing the answer you have in mind

The last one is the most reliable. Instead of `I think it is A, is that right?`, ask `Between A and B, which one does the evidence support?`

steps.title: It drops instructions
steps.contentMarkdown:
You set five conditions and three of them hold. The tone matches but the length runs over; the format is right but a banned phrase is in there.

The more conditions you add, the more often this happens. It overlaps with the way the middle of a long context blurs.

The response splits three ways.

- **Set the conditions out as a list.** Do not bury them in a paragraph; put each on its own line. Stating the count helps further.
- **Attach a self check.** `After writing, go through the five conditions one at a time and mark whether each was met.`
- **Split the conditions.** Instead of demanding everything at once, take a draft and then apply conditions while refining it.

Watching which conditions get dropped repeatedly shows you the priority. Any condition that keeps slipping goes at the very end of the request one more time.

steps.title: It is confident without knowing
steps.contentMarkdown:
This is the most dangerous failure. An unsupported answer comes out in exactly the same voice as a supported one.

Certain places see it more often. Regulations specific to one region, the history of a small institution, the details of an old event, a rule that changed recently. The material is thin and the form gets filled in perfectly.

The response is to create somewhere to record uncertainty at the request stage.

- `Mark anything you are not certain of as needs checking`
- `Leave out anything you cannot support`
- `Give a confidence level for each item`

There is a response after the fact too. `Pull only the sentences in the answer above that need fact checking.` Reviewing its own output has limits, but it gives you the starting point for a check list.

In the end the strongest defense is the habit of not reading a confident voice as a signal.

steps.title: Long output loses the opening
steps.contentMarkdown:
Request a long deliverable and it drifts further from the original conditions as it goes. The opening follows instructions, the tone reverts around the middle, and by the end something you banned appears.

This follows naturally from a structure that appends the next token. The sentence just written is close by and the original instruction is far away.

The response is to split.

- Take it section by section, restating the conditions for each section.
- Fix the outline first, then fill sections in one at a time.
- After receiving a long deliverable, take the back half again with the conditions reapplied.

Taking it in pieces is usually faster than receiving one long piece and reworking the whole thing. When the spots needing work cluster at the end, take just that part again.
steps.imageAlt: A mural pattern gradually drifting along a long wall as the painter copies only the immediately previous version

steps.title: The order for tracing a failure
steps.contentMarkdown:
When a result disappoints, tracing back through the prompt usually finds the cause.

- Is the context slot empty. Check whether reader and purpose were written down.
- Is the task pinned to a verb. Check whether you wrote a topic and stopped there.
- Was the format specified. Leave it open and it changes every time.
- Were constraints written. Skip what to avoid and default habits come through.
- Were examples supplied. Whatever resists description goes over as an example.
- Were steps specified. Judgments with several conditions need an order.
- Was material supplied. Do not make it work from memory when facts are required.

Everything this course covered is on that list. When failures repeat, walking the list line by line is faster than switching tools.

The next course moves off text and into images, voice, and music.

quiz.question: What is the most reliable way to ask that avoids the tilt toward agreement?
choices: State your own conclusion first and have it confirmed
Withhold the conclusion and ask which of two positions the evidence supports
Repeat the same question several times
Request a longer answer
quiz.explanation: Revealing your answer first creates room for it to accommodate you. Hiding the conclusion and asking neutrally is more reliable.

quiz.question: What is the right response when some of several conditions go unmet?
choices: Blend the conditions naturally into a paragraph
Set the conditions out as a list and have them checked one by one after writing
Add more conditions for emphasis
Remove all conditions and leave it open
quiz.explanation: Putting conditions on separate lines, stating how many there are, and attaching a self check afterward all reduce the dropping.

quiz.question: Why do the original conditions fade in the later part of a long deliverable?
choices: Because of a character limit
Because generation appends the next token, so the sentence just written is close and the original instruction is far
Because a translation stage gets inserted
Because format instructions stop working past a certain point
quiz.explanation: Generation continues from what was already written. As the original instruction recedes its influence shrinks, so split by section and restate the conditions.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: The Media Generative Models Work With
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Text, images, voice, music, video. Each medium is produced in a different way, and the difficulty is not the same across them.
objectives: Tell apart recognizing something and producing it
Get the broad picture of how each medium is generated
Understand why adding a time axis makes the problem harder

steps.title: Choosing versus producing
steps.contentMarkdown:
Deciding whether a photo shows a dog or a cat is not the same kind of work as producing a new photo of a cat.

Choosing has a fixed answer. With two options, a guess is right or wrong immediately, so both training and scoring stay simple.

Producing has no single correct answer. There are endless plausible cat photos. The first problem is deciding what to treat as the answer during training.

The solution differs by medium, but the skeleton is the same. **The task gets rewritten as a small problem that does have an answer.** For text, predict the next word. For images, predict what the frame looks like with a little of the noise removed. Thousands of those small predictions get chained into a finished result.

That single idea sits under every medium.

steps.title: Each medium at a glance
steps.contentMarkdown:
What counts as a unit changes from medium to medium.

| Medium | Unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Text | Token | Compute the probability of the next token and append it |
| Image | The whole frame | Start from noise and clear it away over many passes |
| Voice | Sound features | Text to pronunciation, pronunciation to acoustics, acoustics to waveform |
| Music | Audio or notation | Produce the waveform directly, or produce an arrangement of notes |
| Video | Many frames | Image generation plus the flow of time |

One question splits these approaches. Can the result be built one piece at a time in order, or does the whole thing have to be refined at once?

Text runs front to back. An image has no such order, so the whole frame gets revised again and again. The next lesson looks at that method closely.

steps.title: Time makes it harder
steps.contentMarkdown:
Single images come out well while video stays awkward. The time axis is the reason.

A video is a run of images, but frames produced on their own disagree with each other. A shirt changes color, an object in the background disappears, a face shifts slightly from frame to frame. Human eyes catch this kind of drift very easily.

So consistency across frames has to be handled separately. One approach conditions each frame on the one before it, another trains the model on the time direction as well. The computation also grows with the number of frames.

Music has the same trouble. A few seconds of audio sounds plausible, but a three minute piece loses its structure. The opening and the later part need to remember each other, and that distance is long.

Short works, long falls apart. That tendency shows up across generative media.
steps.imageAlt: A stop-motion worker comparing two identical clay bird puppets that differ only in one wing color

steps.title: Working across media
steps.contentMarkdown:
Current models are not limited to one kind of data. They describe an image, read text and produce a picture, listen to audio and write it out.

The reason goes back to the embeddings from the earlier course. Text becomes coordinates, images become coordinates, and both sit in the same space. Training pushes the coordinates of the word cat and the coordinates of a cat photo close together.

Once the coordinates line up, crossing between media becomes arithmetic. Search for an image with text, find similar images from an image, or use text as the condition for producing an image.

Text guided image generation came from here as well. The coordinates of a sentence become the compass for drawing.

steps.title: What to expect and what not to
steps.contentMarkdown:
Knowing the character of each medium makes it easier to decide where to use it.

**Works well.** Drafts, variations, filling in. Reworking something that exists, or filling an empty area. Background images, rough storyboards, placeholder voice, diagrams for reference material.

**Drifts easily.** Exact lettering, a consistent likeness of one specific person, a requested count, structures that have to be physically sound. Wrong finger counts and garbled signage belong here.

**Breaks with length.** Long video, long pieces of music, consistency across many scenes.

The same list is useful from the audience side. Knowing where the awkwardness comes from makes it quicker to judge what you are looking at. The later part of this course covers those cues separately.

quiz.question: What is the shared idea that turns generation, a problem with no single answer, into something a model can be trained on?
choices: People label every correct answer by hand
It gets rewritten as small prediction problems that do have answers, and the results are chained together
Finished results are stored and retrieved when needed
Outputs are produced at random and a person picks one
quiz.explanation: Next token prediction and noise removal are small problems with known answers. Chaining many of them produces the finished result.

quiz.question: Why is video generation harder than a single image?
choices: It needs a higher resolution
Consistency across frames has to be maintained and the computation grows with the number of frames
It uses more colors
Sound has to be produced at the same time
quiz.explanation: Frames produced independently disagree on clothing color, background objects, and faces. Adding the time axis raises the consistency problem and the computational load together.

quiz.question: Why can a sentence steer image generation?
choices: The sentence is looked up in a dictionary of image descriptions
Text and images were trained together so they share one coordinate space
The letters are written directly into the picture
The sentence is translated and used as the image file name
quiz.explanation: Text and images become coordinates in the same space, with related meanings placed close together. That is why the coordinates of a sentence can set the direction of generation.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: From Noise to Image
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Learning the process of adding noise to an image and running it backwards. This is also where wrong fingers and garbled lettering come from.
objectives: Explain the order in which a diffusion model builds an image
Describe how a sentence sets the direction of generation
Explain common visual errors from the underlying mechanism

steps.title: Learning to erase in order to draw
steps.contentMarkdown:
The idea behind **diffusion** starts with a reversal.

First the image gets destroyed. A little noise is mixed into a photo, then more, then more again. After a few hundred rounds the original is gone and only a grainy field remains. People can produce this process themselves, and the answer is known at every point. The answer is what the frame looked like one step earlier.

The model learns to run that process backwards. Given a noisy frame, it predicts the slightly less noisy version. Because an answer exists, the prediction can be scored.

After training, the order is reversed. Start from pure noise and clear a little away at a time. Around twenty steps in, shapes appear. Keep going and an image emerges.

The problem of producing something from nothing was rewritten as a problem of erasing.
steps.imageAlt: A conservator in an archaeology tent revealing mosaic only where sand has been brushed away

steps.title: The sentence is the compass
steps.contentMarkdown:
Clearing noise on its own produces some image, any image. Getting the one you want takes direction.

That direction is the sentence. As the previous lesson showed, text and images share a coordinate space, so the coordinates of the sentence go in at every denoising step. At each step the frame gets organized toward those coordinates.

One setting shows up often: how strongly the sentence should be followed. Set low, the sentence is treated loosely and results vary widely. Set high, the output sticks to the sentence but the frame can turn stiff or the colors can blow out.

Generating several images from the same sentence gives a different picture every time, because the starting noise differs on each run. Fix the starting noise and a similar image can be produced again. That value is called the seed.

steps.title: Why fingers and lettering go wrong
steps.contentMarkdown:
A diffusion model refines the whole frame at once. That is its strength and its weakness at the same time.

The overall impression settles quickly. A person standing indoors under warm light gets decided in the first few steps.

**Counts and order**, on the other hand, are handled poorly. Five fingers is not a property of the overall impression, it is a local rule. If the hand area gets organized into a plausible texture during denoising, the image finishes with the wrong count.

Lettering is harder. Letters have fixed shapes that must appear in a fixed order, and a single mistake is visible immediately. Recent models draw short phrases fairly accurately, but long sentences and unfamiliar scripts still smear.

The same reason explains why requested counts drift. Ask for seven apples and six or eight is a common result.

steps.title: Space and physics wobble too
steps.contentMarkdown:
Relationships between objects in the frame often fail as well.

**Depth.** Something that should sit behind occludes the object in front, or a shadow falls in a direction the lighting does not support.

**Contact.** A chair leg does not reach the floor, or a held object passes through the hand.

**Period and objects.** A scene set in the Joseon era picks up an item that did not exist then. Things that co-occurred in the training material come along with it.

**Scale.** The sizes of people and objects do not agree.

These errors show up on a close look rather than a first glance. The impression is plausible while the relationships do not hold. It follows from what diffusion does. It organizes plausible texture rather than computing and placing objects by rule.

That is why a step for checking relationships belongs before the output gets used.

steps.title: How to fix it
steps.contentMarkdown:
Several methods recover a broken image.

**Regenerate only part of it.** Mask the hand or the face and denoise just that region, which is inpainting. Everything else stays as it was.

**Fix the starting noise and adjust only the sentence.** If the composition works, hold the seed and change the wording a little. That keeps the whole frame from shifting.

**Supply an underlying sketch.** Draw the pose or composition as lines, or provide a reference image and have the structure follow it. Counts and placement become far more stable.

**Add lettering afterwards.** Do not ask for text inside the image. Have the space left empty and place the type in an editing step.

The last method is the most reliable in practice. In this project as well, the text that appears in videos and cards is not left to image generation. It gets placed when the frame is composed.

quiz.question: How is a diffusion model trained?
choices: It memorizes finished images as they are
It learns to reverse the process of mixing noise into an image
It traces lines drawn by a person
It averages several images stacked together
quiz.explanation: Adding noise step by step is something people can produce, and the answer at each step is known. The model learns to run it backwards, then starts from pure noise and clears it away into an image.

quiz.question: Why does the same sentence produce a different image each time?
choices: The sentence is interpreted differently on each run
The noise at the starting point differs on each run
The model keeps training
The resolution changes automatically
quiz.explanation: Denoising starts from noise that differs every run. Fixing that value produces a similar result again, and the value is called the seed.

quiz.question: When exact lettering is needed inside an image, what is the most reliable approach in practice?
choices: Repeat the words several times in the request
Raise the resolution to the maximum
Leave the space empty and place the type during editing
Ask for the text in English instead
quiz.explanation: Letters need fixed shapes in a fixed order, so leaving them to generation invites errors. Reserving the space and adding type in an edit is reliable.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Synthesizing Voice and Music
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: The three stages that turn text into sound, the consent problem in training on someone else's voice, and the places where awkwardness remains.
objectives: Understand the stages that turn text into sound
Identify the consent problem in reproducing a specific person's voice
Point out where synthetic speech and music go wrong

steps.title: Three stages from text to sound
steps.contentMarkdown:
Reading text aloud breaks into three stages.

**Pronunciation.** Letters become the sounds actually spoken. Judgment starts here. `10%` can be read with a loanword form or a native form, and `2026` can be read as one full number or digit by digit. In Korean, where Sino-Korean words and loanwords mix, the options multiply.

**Acoustic features.** The pronunciation information becomes contours of pitch, duration, and intensity. Where the line rises and where it pauses gets decided here.

**Waveform.** Acoustic features turn into an actual sound wave. The file a person can listen to comes out of this stage.

In practice the first stage gets adjusted most often. Numbers, English words, proper nouns, and units are read incorrectly all the time. The fix is to write the pronunciation out explicitly.

steps.title: Training on someone else's voice
steps.contentMarkdown:
Producing a specific person's voice means training on recordings of that person. It used to take hours of audio. Now a short sample gets somewhere close.

As the technique got easier, the problem got larger. A voice identifies a person. Producing and using one without consent is impersonation, and phone scams using a cloned family member's voice have been reported in several countries.

The working line is clear.

- Do not produce a specific person's voice without their consent
- When consent is given, define the scope of use along with it
- Disclose that the voice is synthetic
- For voice actors and performers, check what the contract covers

Rules are still being settled country by country. When a case looks ambiguous, not proceeding is the safer choice.

steps.title: Where awkwardness remains
steps.contentMarkdown:
The raw sound of synthetic speech has reached a point where it is hard to tell from a person. Listen for a while, though, and awkwardness remains in specific places.

**Breathing.** People inhale and pause. Synthetic speech fills those spots evenly or skips them.

**Stress and phrasing.** What to emphasize and where to break depends on meaning. Get the meaning wrong and the intonation is something no person would produce. Long sentences with several clauses are where this happens most.

**Emotional arc.** Within one sentence the feeling is plausible, but the line running through a paragraph breaks. A sad passage suddenly brightens.

**Repeated sentences.** A person changes intonation the second time. Synthesis repeats the same sentence the same way.

Splitting the script into shorter reads, or marking the break points directly, removes much of this.
steps.imageAlt: A singer taking a breath between lines while the director signals a deliberate pause in the recording studio

steps.title: What music generation handles
steps.contentMarkdown:
Music generation splits into two branches.

**Producing audio directly.** A waveform, or something close to it, comes out at once. Instrument tone and sense of space arrive together, but the result is hard to take apart. Changing one note of one instrument does not work.

**Producing notation.** Notes and chord progressions come out. Editing is free and the performance can be swapped. In exchange, the texture of the final sound depends on separate work.

Either way the weak spot is the same, the **structure** of the piece. A stretch of a few dozen seconds is plausible, but the opening and the later part of a three minute piece do not answer each other. A returning chorus disagrees with the earlier one, or the music circles the same spot without developing.

Knowing the chord progressions and song structures covered in the academy's harmony course makes this drift much easier to hear.

steps.title: What to know as a listener
steps.contentMarkdown:
As generated music and speech become common, listening involves more judgment.

**Look for a label.** More platforms disclose whether audio is synthetic. A missing label does not mean a person made it, but a label that is present is definite.

**Listen for traces of performance.** Human playing leaves small inconsistencies. Timing drifts a little and volume moves. Playing that is too even is a cue. Electronic music made by people is also even, though, so nothing can be concluded from this alone.

**Follow the structure.** Track where the piece is going and you can tell whether it develops.

Detection is not the point. The point is that listening while knowing what you are listening to differs from listening without knowing. Noting this alongside a record lets you trace how your own taste shifted later on.

quiz.question: Which stage of turning text into sound do practitioners adjust most often?
choices: The stage that produces the waveform
The stage that decides how numbers, English words, and proper nouns are pronounced
The stage that sets the volume
The stage that changes the file format
quiz.explanation: Pronunciation is where numbers, units, loanwords, and proper nouns get read incorrectly. The fix is to write the pronunciation out directly.

quiz.question: What standard applies when synthesizing a specific person's voice?
choices: Consent is unnecessary if only a short recording is used
Get the person's consent, define the scope of use, and disclose that the voice is synthetic
There are no constraints as long as the use is not commercial
Recordings that are already public can be used freely
quiz.explanation: A voice identifies a person. Consent, a defined scope of use, and disclosure are the baseline, and the relevant rules are still being settled country by country.

quiz.question: Which of these is least likely to be where synthetic speech still sounds off?
choices: Where breaths and pauses fall
Stress and phrasing in long sentences
The raw audio quality of the sound
The emotional line running across paragraphs
quiz.explanation: Audio quality has reached a point that is hard to tell from a person. The remaining awkwardness sits in breathing, stress and phrasing, emotional arc, and repeated lines.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Where It Fits in Production
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Drafts, backgrounds, captions, and translation get delegated while fact checking and final judgment stay with people. This lesson sets the criteria for the split.
objectives: Distinguish which production stages can be delegated
Identify the stages a person has to hold
Set criteria for assigning work by what the tool does well

steps.title: Split the pipeline and the slots appear
steps.contentMarkdown:
Break down what goes into one video. Research, script draft, fact checking, locking the structure, preparing images, recording voice, captions, editing, review.

The stages differ in character. Research and drafting are high volume and easy to undo. Fact checking and review are low volume and hard to undo when wrong.

Delegation has to be decided stage by stage, not for the pipeline as a whole. Making a video with AI is not a thing that actually happens. Which stage was handed over is the whole story.

One criterion helps. **Can a mistake be caught?** Delegate the stages where mistakes surface. Hold the stages where a mistake can pass by quietly.

steps.title: Stages worth delegating
steps.contentMarkdown:
The places with real payoff are specific.

**Drafting.** It removes the cost of starting from an empty screen. Even a weak draft speeds things up once there is something to revise.

**Background and prop images.** Backgrounds, textures, and props are more forgiving than faces or one specific person.

**Caption and translation drafts.** Transcription and timing are tedious for people and machines do them well. For translation, delegate the draft only and let a person handle nuance.

**Organizing reference material.** Pulling items out of a long document into a table. The original sits right there, so checking is easy.

**Making variants.** Producing several versions of the same content at different lengths or in different registers.

They have something in common. A person can look at the result and judge it right away, and mistakes are easy to undo.

steps.title: Stages a person has to hold
steps.contentMarkdown:
The other side is just as clear.

**Fact checking.** People, dates, quotations, figures. As the earlier course showed, invented material and accurate material arrive in the same tone. Delegate the check and the check stops existing as a step.

**Deciding what to make.** Which subject to cover, which passage goes first, what gets cut. The character of the result is decided here.

**Setting the tone.** How to treat the work. How far to go in a passage dealing with someone's death, for instance.

**Final review.** Before publishing, a person looks at the whole thing.

This project uses the same arrangement. Anecdotes and quotations about a person are accepted as data only after an independent check, and generated images are reviewed by eye right after they come out, with anything off in period or spatial terms dropped from the candidates.
steps.imageAlt: An art director removing the only modern unmarked clear water bottle from an otherwise coherent period set

steps.title: The trap of spending more time fixing
steps.contentMarkdown:
Sometimes delegating makes things slower. A few signals give it away.

**The fixes are scattered.** Ten small corrections take longer than writing it yourself. That differs from one large correction in one place.

**The request grows longer than the output.** Writing out every condition means the work is already done. This comes up with short lines and single titles.

**Catching the errors takes expert knowledge.** Here the review burden exceeds the production burden.

**The same correction has been given three times.** That signal appeared in the earlier course. Handle that spot by hand.

When the call is unclear, measure it once. Time the delegate and fix route against doing it directly. Judged by feel, the answer usually tilts toward delegating.

steps.title: What to disclose and what to keep
steps.contentMarkdown:
Two things should be settled before publishing.

**A disclosure standard.** Decide which stages you will disclose. Platform rules differ and keep getting more specific. Parts that could be taken for a person, such as voice or images of people, are safer disclosed.

**Records.** Keep what was used at which stage and under what settings. It lets you trace a problem later, and it also serves when the same result has to be produced again. Storing the request text and the settings next to a generated image file is a common approach.

Settling both at the start removes the need to reconstruct anything later. Working out after the fact what was used where is close to impossible.

quiz.question: Which criterion works for deciding whether to delegate a production stage?
choices: Whether the workload is large or small
Whether a person can catch a mistake
Whether the work is interesting or tedious
How large the budget is
quiz.explanation: Stages where a mistake can pass by quietly stay with people. Stages whose results can be judged right away and undone easily get delegated.

quiz.question: Why should fact checking not be delegated?
choices: Because it becomes slower
Because it costs too much
Because invented and accurate material arrive in the same tone, so the check stops existing as a step
Because there is no search function
quiz.explanation: The purpose of a check is to filter out what is wrong. If the filter shares the same characteristic, the step does not hold.

quiz.question: Which is a signal that delegating is actually slowing you down?
choices: The result is badly off in one single place
Writing out every condition makes the request longer than the output
The result came out in the format that was specified
Several drafts arrived at once
quiz.explanation: For short lines or a single title, writing out the conditions means the work is already done. Corrections scattered across many spots are the same signal.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Copyright and Training Data
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Rights in the material used for training, and rights in what gets generated. This lesson separates the open questions from the working standards available now.
objectives: Identify what is disputed about training data rights
Understand why ownership of generated work is not simple
Set working standards a user can follow now

steps.title: Stated up front
steps.contentMarkdown:
This lesson is not legal advice. It goes only as far as introducing what is disputed.

The relevant rules differ by country and are still changing. Litigation is under way in several places and some matters have come out differently in different jurisdictions. Carrying any one decision over as a settled rule would soon be wrong information.

So this lesson covers two things. What is being argued about, and what attitude a user can reasonably take while the arguments are unresolved.

If an actual decision is needed, check with a professional and with official sources in the relevant country. For commercial use in particular, a platform's terms of service have to be read as well.

steps.title: What is disputed about training material
steps.contentMarkdown:
Generative models train on large volumes of text, images, and audio. A substantial share of that material is under copyright.

The dispute divides roughly like this.

- **Is training itself a use?** One side sees it as equivalent to a person reading a book and learning. The other side holds that copying and bulk processing make it different.
- **Does the output substitute for the original?** There is an argument that reproducing a particular artist's style, and reducing that artist's work as a result, changes the character of the activity.
- **Consent and compensation.** Whether those who supplied the material agreed in advance, and whether they should be paid.
- **Can removal be demanded?** Extracting material already trained into a model is technically hard.

Approaches differ by country. Some allow analysis of material for research broadly, and some are moving toward requiring stronger consent from rights holders.

steps.title: Rights in what gets generated
steps.contentMarkdown:
Rights in generated work are also still being settled. Three questions are tangled together.

**Is it a human creation?** Copyright generally attaches to human creation. How much human authorship goes into a result produced from one sentence is judged differently in different places. There are cases where a small human contribution was held not to qualify for protection.

**Whose is it?** The relationship among the user, the service provider, and the suppliers of training material is mostly set by terms of service. Those terms differ by service, and sometimes by whether the tier is paid or free.

**Does it infringe someone else's rights?** If the output resembles a particular work, that is a problem independent of ownership. The same applies when a real person's face or a trademark ends up in the result.

The third one is the most direct for a user. Something you generated cannot be used if it resembles someone else's work.

steps.title: Working standards for now
steps.contentMarkdown:
Even with the questions unresolved, there is a line that can be held.

- **Decide the use first.** Personal practice and commercial use have different requirements. For commercial use, check terms and licenses before starting.
- **Do not name living artists.** Requests that summon a specific artist's style by name carry high dispute risk. Describing the qualities you want is safer.
- **Avoid real people and trademarks.** A recognizable face, a logo, or a character in the output brings a separate set of rights into play.
- **Check for resemblance.** Search and compare to see whether the result looks like an existing work.
- **Keep the provenance.** Record which tool made it and under what conditions. The need to explain does come up.

The last item connects to the record keeping habit from the previous lesson. What is not kept at production time cannot be reconstructed afterwards.
steps.imageAlt: A designer composing an original abstract resin-and-metal still life without brands, people, or characters

steps.title: Noting it in a record of what you consumed
steps.contentMarkdown:
There is something to settle on the audience side too. How to note a work that generative tools took part in.

The workable approach is to write down facts only. If the stages where it was used are known, carry that over. If they are not known, write that it is unknown. Do not decide by guesswork.

One difficulty is that the degree of involvement often is not published. Whether it went into part of a background or produced the whole thing cannot be determined. So a binary of used and not used does not work well.

This project chose to keep records for its own productions. What was used at which stage goes into the work log, and fact checking runs separately through a person. For outside works, only confirmed facts get written down.

quiz.question: Which of these is not part of the dispute over training data rights?
choices: Whether training counts as a use of a copyrighted work
Whether the output takes the place of the original
Whether rights holders need to consent and be compensated
Whether the model computes quickly enough
quiz.explanation: The disputed points are the nature of training, substitution effects, consent and compensation, and whether removal after the fact is possible. Compute speed has nothing to do with rights.

quiz.question: Among the questions about generated work, which one affects a user most directly?
choices: Whether the output resembles an existing work, a real person, or a trademark
Who paid for training the model
Which country the service's servers are in
What file format the output is in
quiz.explanation: Separately from ownership, resemblance to an existing work, a real person, or a trademark is a problem in itself. It is also the part a user can check directly.

quiz.question: How can risk be reduced in an image generation request?
choices: Name several living artists together
Describe the qualities you want and avoid naming a specific artist
Supply a photo of a real person as reference
Provide an image containing a trademark as reference
quiz.explanation: Requests that summon an artist's style by name carry high dispute risk. Describing the qualities you want directly is safer.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: An Eye for Generated Work
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: The cues that commonly remain and the limits of those cues. Checking where something came from is more reliable than trusting a detection tool.
objectives: Identify the cues that commonly remain in each medium
Understand the limits of detection tools and the risk of false calls
Explain why checking provenance beats reading cues

steps.title: Start by not concluding
steps.contentMarkdown:
One thing has to be settled first. The cues below raise probability. They are not criteria for a verdict.

Some pictures with wrong hands were drawn by people. Plenty of people write smooth prose. In the other direction, generated work without a single flaw is common. Generation tools improve quickly, so a cue that worked yesterday may not work today.

One judgment is especially risky. Pointing at something a person made and calling it generated. Student assignments and artists' work have been suspected without grounds, and it has caused real harm.

So the conclusion of this lesson can be stated in advance. **Read cues as reference and judge by provenance.**

steps.title: What commonly remains in images
steps.contentMarkdown:
This follows from the mechanism in the earlier lesson. The overall impression is accurate while local rules wobble.

- **Counts.** Fingers, teeth, stairs, windows. Things you only know by counting.
- **Lettering.** Signs, book covers, text on clothing. Short words come out right, sentences smear.
- **Symmetry.** Earrings differ left and right, the arms of a pair of glasses do not match, a pattern fails to continue.
- **Contact.** Hand and object, chair and floor, seams in clothing.
- **Shadows and reflections.** A direction that does not match the light source, or a mirror showing something else.
- **Background detail.** Faces in the distance, crowds, and foliage turn mushy.

A fixed order of checks is faster. Take in the whole frame first, then look at what requires counting and what requires reading. After that, check whether the relationships hold.

steps.title: In video and audio
steps.contentMarkdown:
Video is watched along its timeline. The consistency problem from the earlier lesson shows up directly.

- Clothing color, hair length, and background objects change while a shot continues
- A face wavers slightly, or an outline blends into the background
- Walking and hand movements look physically off
- Mouth shapes and sound do not line up

For audio, listen to the places already covered. Breathing, stress, emotional arc, repeated phrasing.

Deepfakes aim at a fixed set of situations. **Urgent requests, money, identity checks.** A call demanding an immediate transfer, an instruction from someone posing as a manager, an emergency involving family.

Analyzing cues is of little use there. Hanging up and calling back on a number you already have is far more reliable. Some households and organizations agree on a verification method in advance.
steps.imageAlt: A woman ending a suspicious smartphone call, placing it face down, and verifying through a separate corded phone

steps.title: The limits of detection tools
steps.contentMarkdown:
Several tools claim to detect generated work. Treating their output as a verdict is risky.

Errors run both ways. Text written by a person gets flagged as generated, and generated text passes as human. Writing by people who are not native speakers has been reported to draw false flags more often.

There is a deeper difficulty. A detector is also a device that reads statistical traits, and generation keeps improving in the direction of removing those traits. It is a chasing structure, so staying ahead is hard.

A different approach has emerged, marking things at production time. An invisible pattern can be embedded as a watermark, and specifications for attaching provenance information to a file are under discussion. That side is more definite, but it goes inert when the mark is stripped or a tool that ignores the specification is used.

Neither side is comprehensive. That is the current state.

steps.title: Judging by provenance
steps.contentMarkdown:
The most reliable method looks at the path rather than the content.

- **Look at who posted it.** Account history, when it was created, other posts.
- **Find the original.** Reverse image search for the earliest posting. For a news photo, check whether news organizations covered it.
- **Confirm through another path.** A major event gets covered in many places. One source alone is grounds for doubt.
- **Look at the context.** Old photos circulating as new events are common. Nothing has to be generated for the claim to be false.

The last item is easy to miss. Real photos spreading with wrong captions occur more often than generated ones. Focusing on detection can mean missing that whole category.

In the end the checking process lands in the same place as the verification habit from the earlier course. Find the grounds and open the original yourself.

quiz.question: What is the right attitude toward cues in generated work?
choices: Treat a single cue as confirmation that it was generated
Read cues only as signals that raise probability and judge by provenance
Treat the absence of cues as confirmation that a person made it
Accept a detection tool's result as the final verdict
quiz.explanation: Work made by people contains errors too, and generated work may contain none. Cues are reference. The judgment comes from the path and the source.

quiz.question: What is the most reliable response to a scam using a deepfake voice?
choices: Analyze the audio quality closely during the call
Run the recording through a detection app
Hang up and call back on a number you already have
Ask the caller a difficult question
quiz.explanation: When an urgent request and a money transfer are involved, cue analysis is of little use. Switching to a different path to confirm is reliable.

quiz.question: Which kind of false information is easy to miss while focusing on detection?
choices: A generated image with smeared lettering
A real photo spreading with a wrong caption
Clothing color changing within a video
Speech with no breathing in it
quiz.explanation: Old photos circulating as new events are more common than generated ones. Looking only at whether something was generated misses this category entirely.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: Where Bias Comes From
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Skew in training material, gaps in how much material each language has, convergence toward majority taste. This lesson looks at what drops out of the results.
objectives: Distinguish the three paths by which bias arises
Identify the effect of unequal material across languages and regions
Judge what bias hides in recommendations and in what you consume

steps.title: What is in the material shows up in the results
steps.contentMarkdown:
A model extracts patterns from material. If the material leans one way, the lean gets extracted with it.

Ask for a picture of a nurse and one gender tends to appear. Ask for a chief executive and a different one does. There were more photos like that in the material. The model did not make a judgment, it reproduced a distribution.

Names show the same thing. Some names appear more often alongside particular occupations or regions, and that link rides along into the output.

Correcting it is difficult too. Removing a particular combination from the material throws something else off, and forcing diversity at the output stage can make historical scenes incoherent. There have been cases where such an adjustment caused real problems.

Bias is not a switch that a setting turns on and off.

steps.title: Languages with much material and languages with little
steps.contentMarkdown:
Differences in how much material exists per language turn into differences in performance. English material dominates, a handful of major languages come next, and the rest have far less.

Several effects follow.

- The same question asked in English sometimes gets a more detailed answer
- People, events, and institutions from languages with less material come out blurry
- Where judgment depends on cultural context, English language norms show up as the default
- Nuance and idiom in languages with less material sound off

The tokenization issue from the earlier course compounds this. Languages with less material get split into more tokens, which also costs more.

Subjects that Korean material mostly carries, such as modern Korean history or domestic institutions, need denser checking.

steps.title: Convergence toward the average
steps.contentMarkdown:
There is another kind of bias, the pull toward majority taste.

In a structure that picks what comes next by probability, common expressions are more likely to be selected. Low probability expressions get pushed out. Results tilt toward the smooth and unobjectionable.

The preference tuning stage pushes the same way. Whatever most raters marked as good becomes the default.

In creative work this is a problem. Getting the common thing means everyone else gets it too. Work made with the same tools starts to resemble itself.

The response is to scatter the direction at the request stage. Write that unobjectionable answers are excluded, or specify several directions and take each one separately. Asking for multiple candidates, from the earlier course, gets used here.

steps.title: What recommendations erase
steps.contentMarkdown:
Recommendations show the same property. Frequently mentioned works get recommended often, and rarely mentioned works get treated as though they do not exist.

Certain places take the hit.

- Works with few translations. Strong reception does not help if mentions are few
- Old works and very recent ones. The first have thin material, the second run into the knowledge cutoff
- Work from smaller regions
- Works inside a genre. Only the landmark titles come back repeatedly

The result is a recommendation list filled with what is already famous. Not a wrong list, but a narrow one.

The response is to narrow the conditions. Specify region, period, language, or scale and a different list comes out. Asking explicitly for titles that are not famous also works.

steps.title: Tracing what got left out
steps.contentMarkdown:
When looking at a result, checking what is absent rather than what is present exposes the bias.

A fixed checklist helps.

- Whether regions are clustered on one side
- Whether periods are clustered in one span
- Whether gender and background lean one way
- Whether only familiar names appear and unfamiliar ones do not

This project carries the same problem. Collecting material about people tilts the list toward regions and eras with plentiful material, and that narrows the range of what gets recorded as well. That is why filling in by region and era is handled as separate work.

There is no method yet for removing bias. Knowing which way the lean runs and covering the other side deliberately is the response available now.
steps.imageAlt: A curator filling an empty space in a moth drawer dominated by one species with a different specimen

quiz.question: Why does gender come out clustered on one side when a particular occupation is requested?
choices: Because a rule is written telling the model to judge that way
Because the distribution in the training material leans one way and the model reproduces that distribution
Because the request was too short
Because the image resolution was low
quiz.explanation: The model reproduces the distribution held in the material rather than making a judgment. Skew in the material comes out as skew in the result.

quiz.question: Why do results tilt toward the unobjectionable and resemble each other?
choices: Because the model stores the same answer
Because common high probability expressions are easier to select and preference tuning pushes the same way
Because the request is long
Because it passes through a translation step
quiz.explanation: In a structure that selects by probability, common expressions have the advantage, and human preference tuning makes what most raters liked the default.

quiz.question: How do you respond to bias in a recommendation list?
choices: Repeat the same question several times
Narrow the conditions by specifying region, period, or language
Ask for a longer list
Take the answer in English
quiz.explanation: Without narrowed conditions the list fills with frequently mentioned works. Specifying region, period, and scale produces a different list.

AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.title: What Stays With People
AI_ACADEMY_LESSONS.description: Taste, the decision about what to make, and responsibility for the result. This lesson locates what cannot be delegated.
objectives: Explain structurally why taste does not transfer
Locate the decision about what to make
Assign work based on where responsibility lands

steps.title: It reports the average
steps.contentMarkdown:
Ask which film to watch and an answer comes. That answer leans toward what is mentioned often in the material and rated well by many. It is the convergence property from the previous lesson.

A majority rating is not your taste. It overlaps sometimes, and that is coincidence.

Taste does not reduce to data. A passage someone found dull is where another finds something, and a widely praised work can fail to reach you. That judgment comes out entangled with a person's experience, the situation at that moment, and everything seen before.

A model has no access to that entanglement. Given the records a user has left, it estimates within them. Without records there is no material to estimate from.

So records come first. Only someone who has written down what they saw and what they felt can work with their own taste.

steps.title: People decide what to make
steps.contentMarkdown:
Break the production process apart and the slots that do not transfer become visible.

Which subject to cover, what to put first, what to leave out. These decisions set the character of the result. Execution can be handed over, but hand over these decisions and nothing is left.

Deciding what to cut is especially like this. Feed in the material and delegate the organizing, and everything comes back included. The human job is choosing what to discard. The standard for discarding is not in the material, it is in the purpose of the person making the thing.

The four part request from the earlier course said the same thing. Writing down context and constraints is the act of deciding. Writing a good request means having made the decisions clearly.

steps.title: Responsibility does not transfer
steps.contentMarkdown:
When something goes wrong with the result, the tool is not an available explanation. Text carrying a false fact, an image infringing someone's rights, a report holding a wrong judgment. Responsibility stays with whoever published it.

The criteria in this course all collapse into one line. **Who answers for it when it is wrong?** If the answer is you, you hold the checking step yourself.

In practice the principle appears as an arrangement.

- Fact checking is done by a person against the original source
- A person approves before any action that is hard to undo
- Before publishing, a person looks at the whole thing
- What was used at which stage is kept in a record

All four appeared in earlier lessons. Rules that looked scattered come from one reason.
steps.imageAlt: A printmaker inspecting the first abstract proof while holding the press lever before a large edition begins

steps.title: What records do
steps.contentMarkdown:
Writing down what you read, watched, and listened to is worth more under current conditions.

**It becomes material for estimation.** Without your own records no tool can work with your taste. You get the average.

**It shows change.** Put your reaction to the same work five years ago next to your reaction now and you can see where you moved. Only someone who kept records has this.

**It becomes grounds for judgment.** As what worked for you accumulates, choosing a new work gets a standard.

Records do not have to be long. What you saw and which part stayed with you, one or two lines, is enough. Even if the summary is delegated, which part stayed is something you have to write yourself for it to mean anything. Fill that spot with someone else's sentences and the purpose of the record is gone.

steps.title: Closing the course
steps.contentMarkdown:
Here is what the three courses covered.

The first course looked at structure. Training and inference are separate, text gets split into tokens, attention captures context, and the next token gets appended. Hallucination grows out of that structure.

The second course dealt with requests. Fill the four parts, give examples, split the work into steps, attach a verification step.

The third course looked at outputs. How images and sound are produced, the rights questions, the limits of detection, the paths bias travels.

The three courses meet in one place. Knowing the mechanism lets you decide for yourself how far to trust a result, and that decision determines how the tool gets used.

The other subjects in the academy are laid out the same way. Light and composition in video, harmony in music, the systems behind books. Knowing the mechanism changes what you see.

quiz.question: Why can taste not be delegated?
choices: Because the technology is not good enough yet
Because a majority rating differs from an individual's taste, and individual judgment comes out entangled with that person's experience
Because taste cannot be built from data, which makes recommendation itself impossible
Because computing taste takes too long
quiz.explanation: What a model returns is what is mentioned often and rated well by many. Individual judgment emerges from experience and situation, so it cannot be handled without your own records.

quiz.question: Which is least likely to be a decision a person has to make during production?
choices: Which subject to cover
What to put first
What to leave out
Transcription and caption timing
quiz.explanation: Choosing the subject, the arrangement, and what to discard creates the character of the result. Transcription and timing can be checked right away, which makes them good candidates for delegation.

quiz.question: Which assignment criterion recurred throughout this course?
choices: How much it costs
How long the work takes
Who answers for it when it is wrong
How long the output is
quiz.explanation: Fact checking, approval points, final review, and record keeping all come from this criterion. When responsibility lands on you, you hold the checking step yourself.
